Among these, those that arise from asceticism are abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*); this applies likewise up to the path (*mārga*).

The others are abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-prahātavya*). Regarding the lower suffering (*adho-duḥkha*), it is present in all [realms]; it is dissociated from three views and functions in two [realms].
The Path eliminates the two views; hatred does not operate in the upper realms.
Regarding "suffering at the bottom for all": suffering at the bottom refers to the suffering of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*); therein, all ten afflictions (*kleśa*) operate.
Ordinary fools do not understand the cause of suffering in the desire realm; seeing it as something to be abandoned, they fall into [the extreme of] annihilationism.
Not understanding its fruit, they see it as permanent;
by slandering the fruit and slandering suffering, they fall into wrong view.
Regarding painful feeling, the first [affliction] is the view of grasping at extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*);
regarding phenomena, to conceive of what is not a cause as a cause is the view of grasping at precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*).

To desire one's own views and to feel aversion toward the views of others, or to give rise to pride (*māna*) from within these views or from one's own views, and the lack of clear comprehension (*avidyā*), are [the afflictions].
Regarding the separation from the two types of practice associated with the three views: there are seven practices each for origination (*samudaya*) and cessation (*nirodha*).

The view of a self (*satkāya-dṛṣṭi*) operates upon the five aggregates manifest in the present; however, because the aspect of origination is subtle and not manifest, the view does not operate therein.
Cessation is also like this.

Those who hold extreme views (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*) also operate within the present; those who hold the view of precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) operate within the realms (*dhātu*). These too are not the cultivation of cessation.

Regarding the Path (*mārga*), it excludes the two views: the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and extreme views do not operate upon the Path, because they have outflowing objects (*sāsravālambana*) as their domain.
The "clinging to precepts" (śīlavrataparāmarśa) proceeds along the path; because it resembles the path, one ultimately fails to understand and does not perceive the true path.

Regarding the absence of ill-will (*vyāpāda*) in the higher realms: as was analyzed for the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), so it is for the form and formless realms (*rūpa-ārūpyadhātu*); with the exception of ill-will, there is no ill-will therein, because the mental application (*manasikāra*) is gentle and supple.

The various views (*dṛṣṭi*) and doubt (*vicikitsā*) are not abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*); the remaining [afflictions] of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) are abandoned through cultivation; those of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) are three; and those of the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) are two.
Question:
How do they take their objects (*ālambana*)?
Answer: Pervasive [defilements] reside in the cause of suffering—namely, doubt, views, and ignorance;
these are the universal latent tendencies (*anuśaya*), while those that take pleasure [in their objects] reside within a single stage (*bhūmi*).

The seeds abandoned through the vision of suffering and those abandoned through the vision of origination, as well as doubt, views, and ignorance—these afflictions are universal; they operate throughout all five categories within their own realm.
Why is this so? Because all contaminated phenomena (*sāsrava-dharma*) have the nature of suffering and its origin (*duḥkha-samudaya*).
Question:
Why do they operate within their own stage and not in other stages?
Answer: Because it is not their objective sphere, they do not operate in higher stages.
Because they are free from desire, these do not operate in the lower realm.
These are called the eleven universal afflictions of the desire realm.
It is the same for the form and formless realms.
The others are not omnipresent, because they have their own seeds as their objects.
The first afflictions are of five kinds; four are said to be the second [category], having the higher realms as their objects, as taught by the Unattached One.

The false view abandoned through the vision of suffering in the desire realm; the adherence to views that slanders the suffering of the form and formless realms; the adherence to precepts and vows as supreme; doubt regarding the means to liberation; and ignorance which lacks clear understanding.

One sees and abandons the false view of grasping at views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*) that slanders the causes of the form and formless realms, taking them to be the primary cause; as well as doubt and ignorance regarding them.
This applies to all stages of the form and formless realms, up to the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*).
Wrong view and doubt are innate (*sahaja*), as is the unshared ignorance (*āveṇikāvidyā*);
they are abandoned by both the path of cessation (*nirodha-mārga*) and the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*). One should know that these have the untainted (*anāsrava*) as their object.
Wrong view abandoned through the vision of cessation (*nirodha-darśana-prahātavyā mithyādṛṣṭi*) slanders cessation; because it takes cessation as its object, it has the untainted as its object.
In this way, doubt regarding cessation and the ignorance associated with it take the untainted as their object.
Likewise, the non-common ignorance abandoned through the vision of cessation—namely, the lack of desire for nirvana—also takes the untainted as its object.
The abandonment through the path of seeing is likewise so.
These eighteen underlying tendencies have the untainted as their object.
Question:
How are the seeds of the outflows bound by the various latent proclivities? Answer:
If the seeds reside in the desire realm, they are bound by all the universal latent proclivities.
The fetters of objects pertain to their own level; it is likewise for those in the higher realms.
All pervasive latent tendencies (sarvatraga-anuśaya) act as fetters through all modes within their own respective levels.
As for the remaining fetters (*saṃyojana*), one should know that they are driven by their own seeds as conditions within their own realm, as well as by those of the associated category.

Regarding the statement "the remaining fetters should be known as being driven by their own seeds as conditions within their own realm": all non-universal fetters (*asarvatraga*) are driven within their own seeds; when they take various phenomena as objects, they are driven by those very [seeds].

Regarding those factors that are associated with this [category]: whether they are universal (*sarvatraga*) or non-universal (*asarvatraga*), they are all driven by association (*saṃprayoga-saṃyojana*) within their own respective categories.

Furthermore, those that operate within the untainted (*anāsrava*) realm, as well as those that take other stages as their objects and cause affliction, are driven by association because their objects are liberated [from such afflictions].

If the outflow-free (anāsrava) objects of engagement and the afflictions (kleśa) that take other stages as their objects are driven by association (saṃprayoga), then if those underlying tendencies (anuśaya) take the outflow-free or higher stages as their objects, they are driven by association within their own category, not by way of being objects of perception (ālambana-anuśaya).
Why is this so? Because of liberation from objective spheres (*viṣaya*).

These latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) do not take objective spheres as their condition; rather, all untainted phenomena (*anāsrava-dharma*) liberate one from all afflictions (*kleśa*), and phenomena of the higher stages liberate one from the afflictions of the lower stages.
Question:
Should these latent tendencies (anuśaya) be described as unwholesome (akuśala) or as indeterminate (avyākṛta)? Answer:

The view of self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*), as well as the ignorance associated with them, are indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) within the realm of desire; this applies to all [such factors] in the realms of form and formlessness.

Regarding "the view of self-identity and the view of extremes, as well as the ignorance associated with them, are indeterminate within the realm of desire": in the desire realm, the view of self-identity, the view of extremes, and the ignorance associated with them are indeterminate.
Why is this? Because the view of a self (satkāyadṛṣṭi) is practiced repeatedly.
If it were unwholesome, sentient beings in the desire realm would have no happiness, for they perform many unwholesome acts.

Furthermore, if it were unwholesome (*akuśala*), it would be contrary to merit (*puṇya*). In this context, one conceives of a self and a person who performs meritorious deeds so that they may obtain happiness.
Since the unwholesome is contrary to the wholesome, the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) is therefore not unwholesome.
The view of annihilationism is the view of non-existence; aversion toward birth and death is likewise not unwholesome, and for this reason it is not unwholesome.
The view of eternalism also does not contradict what is wholesome, just like the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*); therefore, it is not unwholesome.
The remaining afflictions of the desire realm are exclusively unwholesome.
Regarding "all those of the form and formless realms," the various underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) of the form and formless realms are entirely indeterminate (*avyākṛta*). Why is this so?
Because it is destroyed by meditative attainment (*samāpatti*).
As for the unwholesome, one receives the retribution of painful suffering, yet within that [state], there is no painful suffering.
Question:
Do all afflictions bind their own respective objects? Answer:
Greed, hatred, and pride are known to bind what is past.
One receives all [fetters] in the future; for the other two time periods, they are received in their entirety.

Regarding "greed, hatred, pride, and ignorance are known as past fetters": this refers to past craving (*rāga*), hatred (*dveṣa*), and pride (*māna*). It is not necessarily the case that one gives rise to craving toward all objects previously encountered; one cannot give rise to it toward all phenomena simply because it did not arise when those were not perceived.
Regarding "those that will experience everything in the future," this refers to future craving, aversion, and pride, which bind all contaminated phenomena (*sāsrava-dharma*).
Why is this so? Because they take all contaminated phenomena as their object.

Regarding those that exhaustively receive [the results] of the other two time periods: view, doubt, and ignorance take all phenomena as their general objects; therefore, they bind one to all contaminated (*sāsrava*) phenomena of the past and future.
Because they are currently indeterminate, they are not mentioned.
If they were to possess their own specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*), they should be described as being like those of the past.
Having already explained the objects (*viṣaya*) of the various latent tendencies (*anuśaya*), their sequence shall now be explained.
Successive arising occurs within its own stage, and from the higher stages it also arises in the lower;
this matter should be analyzed. Regarding "successive arising occurs within its own stage":
all afflictions of a given stage serve as the immediate condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*) for the afflictions of that same stage; thus, each one can successively give rise to all others.

Regarding the statement that "birth from a higher stage also produces this [lower state], which should be analyzed": when one dies in the Brahma Heaven and is born successively into any part of the desire realm, if one dies there with a defiled mind, the continuity here will consist exclusively of a defiled mind.
Thus, regarding all these stages, the specific characteristics of the various latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) have already been explained.
Since the Blessed One taught these afflictions in many ways for the sake of conversion, they shall now be analyzed.
Question:
The Blessed One has spoken of seven underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*):
sensual desire, ill will, desire for existence, pride, views, doubt, and ignorance.
What is this? Answer: The five kinds of desire in the realm of desire—these are said to be the latent tendency of sensual craving.
Form and formlessness are as described above; the craving for existence (*bhavarāga*) should be analyzed accordingly.

Regarding the five kinds of sensual desires in the desire realm, these are said to be the latent tendency of sensual craving (*kāmarāgānuśaya*), which is abandoned through the vision of suffering, its origin, cessation, and the path, as well as through cultivation (*bhāvanā*).
Regarding the craving for the form and formless realms that must be analyzed as described above: craving in the realm of form is of five kinds, and it is the same for the formless realm.
Hostility (*pratigha*) is itself the latent tendency of hostility (*pratighānuśaya*); its five kinds are as previously explained.
Arrogance (*māna*) and ignorance (*avidyā*), fifteen in total, reside within the three realms.
Regarding the statement that "hatred itself is the latent tendency of hatred, which is of five kinds as previously explained," it means that ill-will (*pratigha*) is likewise of five kinds.

Regarding the statement that "conceit and ignorance (*avidyā*) are fifteen within the three realms," this means that conceit has five kinds in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), five kinds in the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), and five kinds in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*); ignorance is also the same.
The thirty-six proclivities of views (*dṛṣṭi-āsrava*) are said to pervade all three realms;
the twelve proclivities of doubt (*vicikitsā-āsrava*)—these seven have alternative names.

Regarding the statement that the thirty-six proclivities of views pervade all three realms: there are twelve views in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*): five are abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*), two through the vision of origin (*samudaya-darśana-prahātavya*), two through the vision of cessation (*nirodha-darśana-prahātavya*), and three through the vision of the path (*mārga-darśana-prahātavya*).
The same applies to the realms of form and formlessness.

Regarding the twelve latent tendencies of doubt (*vicikitsā-anuśaya*): there are four in the realm of desire, which are abandoned through the vision of suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path; the same applies to the realms of form and formlessness.
Regarding these seven [categories] having different names: these afflictions are called *yoga*, *upādāna*, *āsrava*, and *āśrava*.
Question:
On what basis are they so designated?
Answer: The yokes, the bonds, and the outflows, as well as the taints—all these are endless.
The various yokes, the bonds, and the outflows; these afflictions are what are called "taints" (āsrava).

They are called "yokes" (*yoga*) because they bind all sentient beings; they are called "grasping" (*upādāna*) because they are the instruments for undergoing birth; they are called "flows" (*āsava*) because they cause all sentient beings to flow downward; and they are called "outflows" (*āsrava*) because they leak out endlessly.
Having already explained the various characteristics, the faculties associated with them shall now be discussed.
All latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) within the three realms are entirely associated with the faculties of restraint;
according to their respective levels, these latent tendencies and faculties are associated with the form-body (*rūpakāya*).

Regarding the statement that "all latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) within the three realms are associated with the faculty of guarding (*anurakṣaṇā-indriya*)," this means that all ninety-eight latent tendencies are associated with the faculty of guarding; these various afflictions subsequently cease by relying upon non-seeking (*aniḥsaraṇa*).

Regarding the association of the faculties and underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) with the realm of form (*rūpabhava*) according to their respective stages: in the Brahma-world and the Ābhāsvara realm, there is the faculty of joy (*saumanasyendriya*); the underlying tendencies of those stages are associated with the faculty of joy as well as the faculty of equanimity (*upekṣendriya*).

In the Śubhakṛtsna [heaven], there is the faculty of pleasure; the latent dispositions (anuśaya) of that stage are associated with the faculty of pleasure as well as the faculty of equanimity (*upekṣendriya*).
False view and ignorance, within the desire realm, are associated with both pleasure and suffering;
hatred and doubt are associated only with suffering; it is said that the remainder are exclusively associated with pleasure.

Regarding wrong view and ignorance associated with pleasure and pain in the desire realm: in the desire realm, wrong view and ignorance are associated with the faculty of pleasure and with pain. As for wrong view, it results in joy when one performs unwholesome karma, and it results in grief when one performs pure (wholesome) karma.
The same applies to its association with ignorance.
As for hatred and doubt being associated only with suffering: doubt has dejection as its basis because it is indecisive;
the same holds true for displeasure and hatred.
That is to say, the remaining [afflictions] that are exclusively associated with pleasure (*sukha*) in the desire realm are not associated with suffering; they have joy (*prīti*) as their basis.
The two [types of] clinging and firm attachment to the body, which are abandoned through insight (*darśana-heya*), pertain only to the mind (*manas*).
These are the faculties (*indriya*) that are associated with the various afflictions of the desire realm.

The second type is firmly established through cultivation; it is called the abandonment of all afflictions through contemplation. Among these, there is bodily pain and mental pain corresponding to it.
Of these, bodily pain consists of the faculty of pleasure and the faculty of suffering.
Regarding bodily pain, it is associated with both the faculty of joy (*somanassindriya*) and the faculty of grief (*domanassindriya*).
The faculty of equanimity (*upekkhindriya*) is associated with all bodily pain, as well as with the mental states to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*).

As for those to be abandoned by insight (*diṭṭhi-heya*), they apply only to the mind; that is, the fetters (*saṃyojana*) to be abandoned through the vision of the truths are associated exclusively with the mind.
Those afflictions of the desire realm for which this faculty is the associated [root] are called the afflictions of the desire realm.
Having already distinguished the associated faculties, the higher afflictions shall now be explained.
Lack of shame and lack of dread, sleep, regret, and stinginess, along with envy, restlessness, torpor, and agitation—because these are so prevalent, they are designated as the "higher afflictions.
These eight matters are called the higher afflictions; all the latent tendencies (anuśaya) are afflictions.
Among these, this [defilement] arises from that, and from that it arises; thus, it is a defilement of the underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) and depends upon the underlying tendencies.
Question: What are the defilements of the underlying tendencies?
Answer: It is said that torpor and restlessness are associated with all afflictions;
lack of shame is associated with the unwholesome, and lack of dread is likewise.

When it is said that sleep (*styāna*) and restlessness (*auddhatya*) are associated with all afflictions (*kleśa*), "restlessness" refers to the lack of subsiding within the mind; it is associated with all afflictions, for afflictions themselves are a state of non-subsidience.
Although *middha* (torpor) is called "sinking of the mind," it is also associated with all afflictions (*kleśa*), because a sunken mind gives rise to afflictions.

Regarding the statement that "lack of shame (*āhrīkya*) is concomitant with unwholesome states, and lack of dread (*anapatrāpya*) is likewise": "lack of shame" refers to not feeling shame before others when committing evil.
Lack of shame (*āhrīkya*) is defined as not loathing and not being attached to one's own evil.
These two higher-level afflictions (*upakleśa*) are exclusively associated with the unwholesome (*akuśala*), and are not indeterminate (*avyākṛta*).
That is to say, suffering resides in the mind; regret (*kaukṛtya*) is abandoned through reflection (*vicāra*).
Sleep exists only in the desire realm and in the mental consciousness; the others are each established according to their own nature.

As for suffering, it resides in the mental consciousness and is abandoned through the contemplation of remorse (*kaukṛtya*). Remorse refers to regretting that a good or bad deed was not accomplished; since it cannot be said to be associated with joy, it is invariably associated with suffering.
This [state] is associated with the faculty of mental grief (*daurmanasyendriya*), because it arises from unwholesome conduct (*akuśala-caryā*).
It is said to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*), because it is associated with suffering (*duḥkha*). One should know that this belongs to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).

Regarding the statement that "sleep (*middha*) exists only in the mind of the desire realm": sleep is so called because the mind is closed up; it is invariably located in the mental level (*manobhūmi*) within the desire realm. It is associated with all afflictions (*kleśa*) in the desire realm; indeed, all various afflictions operate during the time of sleep.
Regarding "the others are each established individually," this refers to the remaining two higher-level afflictions:
envy (*īrṣyā*) and avarice (*mātsarya*).
Envy is defined as the arising of feverish distress upon seeing the prosperity of others.
Avarice (*mātsarya*) is defined as guarding, cherishing, and attachment.
It is established as being independent and does not associate with other afflictions.
Question:
With how many consciousnesses are the various afflictions associated? Answer:
Desire, ill-will, and ignorance should be known to depend upon the six consciousnesses.
That is to say, desire is to be abandoned through cultivation; as for form, it is according to what is obtained.

One should know that desire, hatred, and ignorance depend upon the six consciousnesses. "Desire is to be abandoned through cultivation" means that desire in the desire realm is abandoned through cultivation; craving, hatred, and ignorance are associated with the six consciousnesses.
Regarding "whatever is obtained within the realm of form" (*rūpadhātu*): craving and ignorance are obtained according to what is available within the realm of form.

Among the four consciousnesses in the Brahma-heavens, these two afflictions are associated with those four consciousnesses; the remaining afflictions reside within the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).
The various afflictions have already been explained; now their abandonment shall be discussed.
The simultaneous abandonment of afflictions and liberation therein is that which is attained over immeasurable time, as taught by the One of Right Knowledge.

Regarding "those who sever afflictions at once and attain liberation therein": these afflictions are severed in a single moment by the path of non-obstruction (*ānantarya-mārga*); they are not severed again after having already been severed.

Regarding "that which is spoken of as the right knowledge obtained over immeasurable time": this refers to the attainment of the total exhaustion [of outflows] through repeated practice, such as the abandonment of what is to be severed through vision in the desire realm.
In five stages, one attains the realization of one's own portion and the four fruits of śrāmaṇya; all such matters are as explained in the "Chapter on the Noble Ones" (Āryavarga).
Regarding liberation within the desire realm, the Noble Ones speak of four knowledges of abandonment (*prahāṇajñāna*);
regarding the separation from the realms of form and formlessness, one should know there are five knowledges of abandonment.

The permanent exhaustion without remainder is called the knowledge of abandonment (*prahāṇajñāna*). Within this, there is one knowledge of abandonment for the complete liberation attained through the exhaustion of those [defilements] abandoned by seeing suffering and its origin in the desire realm;
two for those abandoned by seeing cessation;
and three for those abandoned by seeing the path.

There are four types of abandonment through reflection (*bhāvanā-heya*): in the form and formless realms, there is one knowledge of abandonment (*prahāṇa-jñāna*) for the abandonment of suffering and its origin (*duḥkha-samudaya-darśana-heya*),
and two for the abandonment of cessation (*nirodha-darśana-heya*).
Three are abandoned by the path of seeing;
four are abandoned by cultivation in the form realm;
five are abandoned by cultivation in the formless realm.
Question:
For what reason is there knowledge of abandonment regarding the section on abandonment? Answer:
Because it is the fruit of wisdom, it is called "knowledge of abandonment.
Just as one born into the Gautama lineage is also called Gautama, so too is this the case.
Question:
Are these proclivities associated with the mind or dissociated from the mind?
Answer: They are associated.
Why is this so? The mind is driven by latent afflictions; it obstructs purity and opposes the attainment of all sublime virtues.
One should know that these are the associated latent tendencies.
Regarding the mind being "associated with the underlying tendencies" (*anuśaya*): if the underlying tendencies were dissociated from the mind, they would not afflict the mind.
Since they do afflict the mind, they are therefore associated.
As for what is called an "obstruction": if the underlying tendencies were dissociated from the mind, they would not obstruct any wholesome dharmas.
If there is an obstruction, wholesome dharmas do not arise.
Because non-obstruction causes them to arise, it is contrary to the aspect of purity.
As for those various sublime and wholesome states that can be attained, if they were not associated with the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*), they would not be in opposition to the wholesome.
If it were not in contradiction with the wholesome, then the wholesome mind would also arise.
If they were not associated, then this nature of affliction would likewise not cause harm.
If they are in contradiction, they constantly follow one another so that the wholesome does not arise; if they are not associated, then the wholesome arises.
For this reason, these are the associated proclivities (*anuśaya*).
Chapter Five: The Noble Ones. Having already explained the Chapter on Proclivities, the Chapter on the Noble Ones shall now be discussed.
Thus the Noble One has severed weariness, the root of all terrors;
through equal skillful means and right wisdom, I shall now speak—listen well.
For one whose mind is not stilled, it is impossible to give rise to right view.
First, from one's own physical basis, bind the mind to make it steady;
likewise, one desires to bind the consciousness firmly and exhaust the enemy of the afflictions.
This is the skillful means regarding the body: its true characteristic is constant stability.
All feelings and this mind, as well as all phenomena, should be viewed in this same way.
This body has the characteristic of impurity, the characteristic of impermanence, the characteristic of suffering, and the characteristic of non-self; these characteristics are certainly real.

Having bound his mind to a single point and become free from mental distraction, he first truly contemplates the characteristics of the body; next, he contemplates sensation; and finally, he contemplates the mind, along with its concomitants, its supports, and the other associated mental factors.
Contemplation is also among the formations dissociated from mind;
according to its nature and according to its characteristic, whatever is thus, that body, sensation, mind, and phenomena arise in correct succession through attention.
Entering into the Dharma through general observation, one observes the common characteristics of all phenomena:
these four are impermanent, empty, non-self, and not pleasant.

Regarding "entering into the Dharma through general observation, observing the common characteristics of all phenomena": this means that within the application of mindfulness to phenomena (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*), the noble one generally observes the characteristics of all conditioned formations (*saṃskāra*).

Having observed the characteristics of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*), one cultivates and increases tranquility (*śamatha*), giving rise to the stainless eye of wisdom (*jñānacakṣus*) to contemplate the body, sensations, mind, and phenomena as a whole. Question: How so?
Answer: These four are impermanent, empty, selfless, and not pleasant.

This body, sensation, mind, and phenomena arise from one another in succession; therefore, they are impermanent. Because they lack autonomy, they are empty. Because there is no master, they are selfless. Because they are evil calamities and afflictions, they are suffering.
From this, what is called the "Heat" (uṣmagata) dharma arises within the mind;
practicing these sixteen aspects, one correctly contemplates the Four Noble Truths.

Regarding the phrase "From this, what is called the Heat dharma arises within the mind": through such contemplation, one generates wholesome heat, within which the fire of untainted wisdom (anāsrava-jñāna) shall arise, capable of burning away the fuel of all conditioned formations (saṃskāra).
Question:
What is its practice and what is its object? Answer:

One practices these sixteen aspects to correctly contemplate the Four Noble Truths. These sixteen aspects have the Four Noble Truths as their objective domain. One contemplates the Truth of Suffering through four aspects:

this nature of suffering is inferior because it arises from causes and conditions and is therefore impermanent; it is suffering because it is destroyed by the power of impermanence; it is empty because it is internally devoid of a person; and it is non-self because it lacks autonomy.

The four modes of contemplation constitute "habituation" (*vāsanā*), because this habituation is the cause that produces a corresponding fruit; it is "existence" (*bhava*) because the continuity of these modes of activity (*ākāra*) results in the obtainment of all births and deaths without end; and it is the "condition" (*pratyaya*) because dissimilar phenomena continue in succession.

One contemplates cessation through four aspects: it is "cessation" because it extinguishes all afflictions; it is "tranquility" because it removes the fires of all defilements; it is "sublime" because it surpasses all phenomena; and it is "renunciation" because it abandons birth and death.

The fourfold path of contemplation: this path is called "path" because it leads to the state beyond categories; it is called "suchness" because it is not inverted; it is called "track" because it is trodden by all noble ones; and it is called "vehicle" because it carries one out from the afflictions of birth and death.
This refers to practicing the sixteen aspects within the sphere of the Four Noble Truths;
these roots of goodness are called the "Heat" (*uṣmagata*) stage.
Once that has arisen and been established, one gives rise to the "Summit" (*mūrdhan*) and the "Patience" (*kṣānti*).
Having attained the Supreme Mundane Dharma (*laukikāgradharma*), one relies upon a single characteristic (*ekalakṣaṇa*).

Once that has arisen, it establishes the "Summits" (*mūrdhan*) and the "Patience" (*kṣānti*). If one has already accomplished the "Heat" (*uṣmagata*) dharma, within that state one further generates roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*) regarding the desire realm that are like the Summits; because they surpass the Heat dharma, they are called the Summits. These likewise involve the sixteen aspects (*ṣoḍaśākāra*) for contemplating the Four Noble Truths.

When one has further increased the "summit" stage, the roots of goodness are called "patience" (*kṣānti*). One also contemplates the Four Noble Truths through the sixteen aspects; it is called "patience" because of its capacity for endurance.

Once patience is established, one attains the "Supreme Mundane Dharma" (*laukikāgradharma*), which relies upon a single characteristic and is the most excellent root of goodness arising among all mundane virtues. This is named the Supreme Mundane Dharma.
Because it opens the gate to *nirvāṇa* and because it is the most supreme within the minds of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), it is called the "Supreme Dharma" (*agradharma*).
Question:
For what reason is it said to rely upon a single characteristic (*ekalakṣaṇa*)?
Answer: Within the minds of ordinary beings, there is nothing comparable to these two qualities.
If there were, they too would open the gate to nirvāṇa, yet they do not. Therefore, it is said that they rely upon a single characteristic.
Question:
How many modes of activity does it have, what is its object-condition, and by which stage is it subsumed? Answer:
Those four aspects of the suffering of conditioned formations (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*) are said to be subsumed under six stages.
Regarding "the suffering of conditioned formations," that refers specifically to the Truth of Suffering as its object, and nothing else.
As for "the four aspects," they refer to taking the Truth of Suffering as their objective domain, with impermanence (*anitya*) at their head.
Why is this so? Just as it is with the initial untainted mind (*anāsrava-citta*), the same applies when taking that [object] as its focal point.
Regarding the statement that they are "subsumed under six stages," those dharmas are subsumed within the six stages.
The preparatory dhyāna (anāgamya), the intermediate dhyāna (dhyānāntara), and the four fundamental dhyānas do not belong to the desire realm, because they are not part of the indeterminate realm;
nor do they belong to the formless realm, because the path of vision (darśanamārga) is absent there.
Question:
By which stages (bhūmi) are the remaining roots of goodness (kuśalamūla) subsumed? Answer:
"Patience likewise encompasses six stages; the remainder relies upon seven. Regarding "patience likewise encompasses six stages":
the Patience of Accordance with Truth (satyānulomikī kṣānti) is encompassed by six stages, just like the Supreme Mundane Dharma (laukikāgradharma).

As for "the others depend on seven," the stages of Heat (ūṣmagata) and Summits (mūrdhan) are subsumed within the seven stages; these six, along with the desire realm when desire has not yet been eliminated, the desire realm when desire has already been eliminated, and the form realm.
Immediately following the Supreme Mundane Dharma (*laukikāgradharma*), the Dharma-patience (*dharmakṣānti*) necessarily arises;
following patience, knowledge (*jñāna*) arises, both of which contemplate the suffering of the lower realm.

Regarding "immediately following the Supreme Mundane Dharma, the Dharma-patience necessarily arises": immediately after the Supreme Mundane Dharma, the untainted (*anāsrava*) Dharma-patience arises, which is termed the "Dharma-patience regarding suffering" (*duḥkha-dharmakṣānti*).

Because he had never previously observed it, but is now capable of observing it at this time, it is called "patience" (*kṣānti*); this is what is meant by the first untainted path of non-obstruction (*anāsrava-ānantarya-mārga*).

Following patience, wisdom arises; that which arises in succession is the "knowledge of the dharma regarding suffering" (*duḥkha-dharma-jñāna*), which shares the same objective sphere and constitutes the path of liberation through the realization of true reality.
Question:
What are the conditions for that patience and wisdom? Answer:
They both observe the suffering of the lower realm;
"suffering of the lower realm" refers to the suffering of the desire realm, which they take as their common object.
The same applies to the suffering of the higher realms, as well as to the causes, cessation, and the path.
This is the correct contemplation of all phenomena; it explains the sixteen moments of pure mind.

Regarding "the higher suffering is also like this": the higher suffering refers to the suffering of the form and formless realms (*rūpa-ārūpya-dhātu*). Therein, there likewise arise the patience of endurance (*kṣānti*), the path of non-obstruction (*ānantarya-mārga*), and the knowledge of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*), as well as the patience regarding the subsequent knowledge of suffering (*duḥkhe 'nvaya-jñāna-kṣānti*) and the subsequent knowledge of suffering (*duḥkhe 'nvaya-jñāna*).

The cause is the truth of origination (*samudaya-satya*); it likewise gives rise to the four paths in the same manner as suffering: the patience regarding the dharma of origination (*samudaye-dharmakṣānti*), the knowledge of the dharma of origination (*samudaye-dharmajñāna*), the subsequent patience regarding origination (*samudaye-anvayakṣānti*), and the subsequent knowledge regarding origination (*samudaye-anvayajñāna*).
Regarding cessation (*nirodha*): cessation likewise gives rise to four paths:

the patience regarding the dharma of cessation (*nirodhadharmakṣānti*), the knowledge regarding the dharma of cessation (*nirodhadharmajñāna*), the subsequent patience regarding cessation (*nirodhānvayakṣānti*), and the subsequent knowledge regarding cessation (*nirodhānvayajñāna*).
Regarding the path (*mārga*) being the same: the path likewise gives rise to four paths.

The patience regarding the dharma of the path (*mārga-dharma-kṣānti*), the knowledge regarding the dharma of the path (*mārga-dharma-jñāna*), the patience regarding the subsequent knowledge of the path (*mārga-anvaya-kṣānti*), and the subsequent knowledge of the path (*mārga-anvaya-jñāna*).
These sixteen pure minds, which consist of the correct contemplation of all dharmas, constitute the vision of the Dharma (*dharma-darśana*).
One who sees the Dharma is said to possess right contemplation; this is another name for such vision.
Those of sharp faculties who proceed by means of the Dharma abide within the fifteen moments of mind;
it should be known that those who proceed by faith also abide therein, as do those of dull vision.

Regarding the statement, "From the dharma-follower with sharp faculties, this occurs within fifteen moments of mind": at the peak of those fifteen moments of mind, if one possesses sharp faculties, they are called a dharma-follower (*dharmānusārin*).

Regarding the statement, "One should know that the faith-follower with dull vision is also included therein": at the peak of those same fifteen moments of mind, if one possesses dull faculties, they are called a faith-follower (*śraddhānusārin*).
Those who have not yet abandoned desire for the realm of desire and are proceeding toward the first fruit abandon six paths and reach two;
those in the three stages of approach possess nine untainted [paths].

Regarding "those who have not yet abandoned desire for the realm of desire and are proceeding toward the first fruit": when those following by faith (*śraddhānusārin*) and those following by dharma (*dharmānusārin*) proceed toward the fruits of śramaṇaship, if they have not yet abandoned desire, both proceed toward the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpattiphala*).

Regarding the abandonment of the six destinies down to two: there are nine grades of afflictions in the desire realm—namely, the lower-lower, the lower-middle, the lower-upper; the middle-lower, the middle-middle, the middle-upper; and the upper-lower, the upper-middle, and the upper-upper.
If, while still an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*), one has already abandoned six types [of afflictions], then upon subsequently attaining realization, one is proceeding toward the second fruit.

Regarding those who possess three stages of approach (*pratipannaka*) and nine untainted paths (*anāsrava-mārga*): if one has already abandoned nine types [of afflictions], one is proceeding toward the fruit of *anāgāmin*.
If one reaches the sixteenth moment of mind, this is called abiding in the fruit.
One who is liberated through faith with weak vision is called "one who has attained vision" (dṛṣṭiprāpta) when their vision is sharp.

Regarding the statement, "If one reaches the sixteenth moment of mind, this is called abiding in the fruit": the sixteenth moments of mind are designated as the mind associated with the knowledge of the path of subsequent cognition (*mārgānvayajñāna*); once that has arisen, one is said to abide in the fruit.
Those who have never yet abandoned the desires of the desire realm are all *srotāpannas*;
those who have already abandoned six grades [of defilements] are all *sakṛdāgāmins*;
and those who have completely abandoned nine grades are all *anāgāmins*.

Regarding the statement that "one liberated through faith is of dull faculties while one who has attained vision is of sharp faculties": when they proceed toward their respective goals, one who follows through faith with dull faculties is "liberated through faith," whereas one who follows through the Dharma with sharp faculties is "one who has attained vision."
"Those who have not yet exhausted the abandonments through cultivation may undergo up to seven births and deaths;
those for whom three [categories of defilements] are exhausted are 'family-to-family' (kulaṃkula); both reside in the fruit of the path of stream-entry.

Regarding "those who have not yet exhausted the abandonments through cultivation may undergo up to seven births and deaths": this refers to those liberated by faith (śraddhādhimukta) and those attained through vision (dṛṣṭiprāpta) who have not yet abandoned the afflictions of the desire realm to be abandoned through cultivation; such individuals will undergo up to seven births and deaths.
Because they have seven more births remaining in the heavens and among humans, it is said that their "maximum births" (parama-saptakṛtvaḥ) consist of seven existences.

Regarding those for whom three [fetters] are exhausted: if the three types—the superior-mild, the superior-middle, and the superior-superior—are exhausted, these are called "those who go from family to family" (kulaṃkula).
In those heavens and among humans, one is born into two or three families before attaining parinirvāṇa; therefore, they are called "family-to-family" (kulaṃkula).

Those who both abide in the fruit of the path of entry (srotāpatti-phala)—namely, those with at most seven more existences and those who are family-to-family—should be said to both dwell as srotāpannas.
Six exhaustions lead to one return; Free from eight, one is called a "once-returner.
The ninth extinction leads to non-returning; One has already emerged from the mire of desire.
Regarding "six exhaustions lead to one return": if there are six types of exhaustion—three of the higher [fetters] and three of the middle—one is a *sakṛdāgāmin* (once-returner).
Having had one remaining birth among the devas and one birth among humans, and having attained parinirvāṇa after one such "coming and going," he is therefore called a Sakṛdāgāmin.

Regarding the statement that one who has abandoned eight [categories of defilements] is a "One-seeded" (Ekabījika): if eight grades are exhausted, one is a One-seeded; because only one birth remains for him and there is no further existence, he is called a One-seeded.
Regarding the ninefold extinction of the non-returner (*anāgāmin*): if all nine grades [of defilements] are exhausted, one is an *anāgāmin*.
Because such a person does not return again to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), they are called an *anāgāmin*.
Why is this so? Because one has already emerged from the mire of desire.
Thus, these nine afflictions, if they exist in the upper eight stages, [are abandoned].
"That which is to be abandoned by the two paths has been taught by the World-Honored One.

Thus, if these nine afflictions exist within the upper eight stages—just as there are nine types of afflictions in the desire realm, ranging from the weakest of the weak to the strongest of the strong—the same applies to the upper realms.

Within these eight stages, they are: the Brahma-world (Brahmaloka), Ābhāsvara, Śubhakṛtsna, Bṛhatphala, the Sphere of Infinite Space (Ākāśānantyāyatana), the Sphere of Infinite Consciousness (Vijñānānantyāyatana), the Sphere of Nothingness (Ākiṃcanyāyatana), and the Sphere of Neither-Perception-nor-Non-perception (Naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana).

Regarding that which is said by the Blessed One to be abandoned by the two paths: all these afflictions of the desire realm, as well as those of the form and formless realms, are abandoned by the two paths; they are eliminated by the path of non-obstruction (*ānantarya-mārga*) and realized through the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*).
Question:
Is this path worldly (*laukika*) or untainted (*anāsrava*)? Answer:
The defiled and undefiled paths are both capable of transcending the eight stages;
one who abides therein is said to be a "body-witness" (kāyasākṣin), meaning they have attained the meditative absorption of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti).
These consist of one stage of the desire realm, four stages of the form realm, and three stages of the formless realm; they are both mundane paths of cessation and supramundane [paths].
If even ordinary persons can achieve detachment through the mundane path, how much more so for those who dwell as noble ones and are said to have realized it bodily?

This refers to those who have attained the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*) and abide within the desirelessness of the eight stages; that is, one who has acquired the absorption of cessation through training is said to be "one who has realized it bodily."
Why is this? Because the Dharma resembles nirvāṇa and is touched by the body, it is called "bodily realization.
Immediately following the diamond-like concentration (vajropama-samādhi), one will necessarily attain the knowledge of exhaustion (kṣaya-jñāna).

"My births are ended; I am free from all outflows. Regarding the statement that "immediately following the diamond-like concentration (vajropama-samādhi), one necessarily attains the knowledge of exhaustion (kṣayajñāna)":

the diamond-like concentration is named after the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana). It is the ninth path of non-obstruction (ānantarya-mārga) at the time of detachment from desire, the final mind of a learner (śaikṣa). Within it, all afflictions (kleśas) are forever exhausted without remainder, and because all noble practices (āryacaryā) have reached their ultimate completion, it is called the diamond-like samādhi. Following this, there arises the knowledge of exhaustion, which is the first knowledge of one beyond learning (aśaikṣa).

When one perceives, "My births are exhausted; I am free from all taints," that concentration of mind is certain: "All my births are exhausted. At that time, being unattached, one is liberated from all taints.
Question:
How many kinds of non-attachment are there? Answer:
There are six kinds of non-attachment; five of these arise from faith, while attaining the two types of knowledge, one should know them as those liberated by time (*samaya-vimukta*).
Regarding "there are six kinds of non-attachment," the World-Honored One spoke of six types of non-attachment:

The dharma of falling away (*parihāṇadharman*), the dharma of mindfulness (*anurakṣaṇādharman*), the dharma of guarding (*anurakṣaṇādharman*), the dharma of abiding equally (*sthitākampya*), the dharma of certain advancement (*prativedhanādharman*), and the immovable dharma (*akopyadharman*).
Among these, if one possesses weak wisdom and weak vigor, one falls away as soon as the conditions for falling away are encountered; therefore, it is called the "dharma of falling away."

One of dull wisdom and dull energy repeatedly manifests an unwholesome body; because one contemplates the destruction of that unwholesome body, it is called "mindfulness of phenomena" (*dharmānusmṛti*).
One of dull wisdom but expansive energy constantly guards the mind through the power of exertion; therefore, it is called "guarding of phenomena" (*dharmanidhyapti*).
Those with middling wisdom and equal progress are neither increasing nor decreasing; because they abide in the Middle Way, they are said to dwell in equanimity (*samavihārin*).
Those with little gain but vast progress will certainly attain immovability; therefore, they are said to be certain of advancement (*niyata-viśeṣa-gāmin*).
Those with sharp wisdom and vast progress are the first to attain immovability; therefore, they are called "immovable.

Regarding the statement that from faith one gives rise to five [faculties] and attains two knowledges: among these, the five previously proceeded by way of faith, and therein there are two knowledges:
the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) and the vision of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa-samyagdṛṣṭi*).
It should be known that one who is liberated by occasion (samaya-vimukta) seeks the occasion; such a person is unable to train in the wholesome at all times as they desire.
One of immovable dharma (akopya-dharman) with sharp faculties is liberated without occasion (asamaya-vimukta);
having attained the three knowledges (trividyā), they achieve equal liberation (sāmāyikī vimukti).

Those of immovable dharma and sharp faculties are those liberated at any time; that is to say, those who are exclusively of sharp faculties and of immovable dharma are liberated at any time, being able to train in the wholesome at all times according to their desire, without seeking a specific occasion.
Regarding "one who has attained the three knowledges," there are three knowledges for such a person:
the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*), the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*), and the right view of one beyond training (*aśaikṣasamyagdṛṣṭi*).

Regarding "one who has accomplished equal liberation," this refers to the five types of liberated ones who are liberated through timely attainment; these are those who have accomplished equal mental liberation (*samacittavimukti*). As for the immovable dharma (*akopyadharman*), they are those who have accomplished immovable liberation (*akopyavimukti*).
One should know that the one liberated by wisdom (prajñāvimukta) does not attain the meditative absorption of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti);
only the one liberated in both ways (ubhayatobhāgavimukta) accomplishes the absorption of cessation.

Regarding the statement "one should know that the one liberated by wisdom does not attain the absorption of cessation": if these six types of non-attached ones (anāgāmin) do not accomplish the absorption of cessation, they are called "liberated by wisdom"; this is liberation through the power of wisdom, not through the power of concentration.

Only those who are liberated through both parts and have accomplished the attainment of cessation—namely, these six types of non-attached ones—if they attain the attainment of cessation, are said to be "liberated through both parts. Their power is twofold:
the power of wisdom and the power of meditative concentration.
Having already explained the noble persons, the Dharma shall now be explained.
From the various dharmas of those who practice through faith, and from the dharmas of those who practice through the Dharma,
the Noble Path and the Path of Seeing the Truths— all these are of one and the same characteristic.
Proceeding from the dharma of faith-practice and proceeding from the dharma of dharma-practice is called the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*).
Among these, the faculties (*indriya*) are called the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (*anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya*);
as for the remaining dharmas of those in training (*śaikṣa*), the Buddha taught them as the faculty of "one who has known" (*ājñendriya*).

Regarding the statement "among these, those dharmas that are faculties are called the faculty of 'I shall come to know the unknown'": within the dharmas of the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), the faculties counted as faculties—namely, mind (*citta*), sensation (*vedanā*), faith (*śraddhā*), and the other four faculties beginning with energy (*vīrya*)—are the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (*anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya*).

When the Buddha says that the remaining dharmas of those in training (śaikṣa) are the faculty of "already known" (ājñātendriya), this refers to the faculty designated as the faculty of "already known" among all those remaining dharmas of training, excluding the dharmas of training belonging to the path of vision (darśanamārga).
One should know that the faculty of "I have known" (ājñātāvīndriya) exists within the state of one beyond training (aśaikṣa);
having attained the fruit, it is then relinquished, and the preceding path should be explained.

Regarding the statement "one should know that the faculty of 'I have known' exists within the state of one beyond training": among the dharmas of one beyond training, that very faculty is designated as the faculty of "I have known."

Regarding the statement that "once the fruit has been attained, one abandons the preceding path," this means that when one ascends to attain a fruit through these untainted (*anāsrava*) dharmas, one abandons those [dharmas] comprised within the path of non-obstruction (*ānantarya-mārga*) as well as the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*).
"Exhaustion is liberation; it is comprised within a single fruit.
It is undefiled as the ninth [moment]; its cessation should be explained.

Regarding "exhaustion is liberation; it is comprised within a single fruit": from the path of non-obstruction (*ānantarya-mārga*) up to the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*), the exhaustion of afflictions (*kleśa-kṣaya*) is attained within that interval.
When the fruit is attained, all afflictions (*kleśa*) are exhausted, and one attains the fruit of liberation.

Regarding the statement that "the ninth undefiled cessation should be explained," this means that while the various afflictions are abandoned by nine types of paths, the ninth undefiled path of non-obstruction (*anantarya-mārga*) abandons [the remaining defilements] all at once, not gradually.
If there is one with a similar name, they are able to attain the immovable, non-attachment, and liberation through faith; such a person increases the path of that same nature.

Regarding "if there is one with a similar name, they are able to attain the immovable": this means that not all who are non-attached (anāgāmin) can attain the immovable state; their nature must necessarily progress further, and attaining that [higher stage] constitutes having a "similar name."

Regarding the statement that "the one without attachment (asaṅga) and the one liberated through faith (śraddhādhimukta) are of the same nature as those who increase the path": this means that the one liberated through faith is invariably destined for progress; they enhance their faculties and attain the state of one who has seen the truth (dṛṣṭiprāpta), whereas others do not.
Question:
How is it known that one perceives the truths gradually? Answer:
Establishing merit and evil, one perceives the truths in succession.

It is not that one perceives evil while perceiving merit, nor does one perceive merit while perceiving evil. Nor is it that one first observes those evils in their entirety, nor is it that one simultaneously feels revulsion for them all, nor is it that one takes all merits collectively; nor do all merits combine at once. Therefore, by establishing merit and evil, one perceives the truths in succession.
Question:
How is it known that there are conditioned and unconditioned fruits? Answer:
Through the power of the path of non-obstruction, one attains conditioned and unconditioned fruits.

Because the power of the path of non-obstruction brings about both conditioned and unconditioned fruits, it is said that through the power of the path of non-obstruction, one attains conditioned and unconditioned fruits.
*Abhidharmahṛdaya-śāstra*, Fascicle Two;
*Abhidharmahṛdaya-śāstra*, Fascicle Three.
Composed by the Venerable Dharmottara.
In the first year of the Taiyuan era of the Jin dynasty,
Saṃghadeva’s wisdom and nature were fully realized; he clearly contemplated all that exists,
as well as non-existence and nirvāṇa— the characteristics of these I shall now explain.
Thus, having briefly explained existence and non-existence in the "Chapter on the Knowledge of the Noble Ones," the objects of that knowledge shall now be discussed.

The Buddha taught three types of knowledge: the supreme and foremost mental states—namely, the knowledge of phenomena (*dharma-jñāna*), the subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*), and conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*).
These three types of knowledge encompass all knowledge; among them, "dharma-knowledge" (dharmajñāna) refers to its objective domain.

It is the untainted knowledge regarding the suffering, origin, cessation, and path within the desire realm; because it first apprehends the characteristics of phenomena (dharmalakṣaṇa), it is called dharma-knowledge.

Having already perceived through the faculty of dharma-knowledge (*dharmajñāna*), one also perceives through non-faculties and through subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*). "Subsequent knowledge" is a name for its objective sphere:

it is the untainted knowledge whose sphere consists of the suffering, origin, cessation, and path of the form and formless realms. Because it subsequently apprehends these dharmic characteristics, it is called subsequent knowledge.

Conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*) refers to contaminated knowledge (*sāsrava-jñāna*), which primarily apprehends things such as the truths of equality, male and female, long and short, and so forth.
Regarding suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path—these two types of knowledge are obtained as they may be;
these are designated as the four knowledges, as taught by the Teacher of Liberation.
Regarding these two knowledges—dharma-knowledge and subsequent knowledge—when they operate upon the truths, they are designated by corresponding names as follows:

that which has the truth of suffering as its object is called knowledge of suffering; that which has the truth of origination as its object is called knowledge of origination; that which has the truth of cessation as its object is called knowledge of cessation; and that which has the truth of the path as its object is called knowledge of the path.
As taught by the Master of Liberation:
if wisdom contemplates the minds of others, it is said to arise from three [knowledges];
the two knowledges of exhaustion and non-arising have the four doors as their objective domain.

If knowledge that contemplates the minds of others is said to arise from these three [knowledges], then the knowledge of others' minds has the outflow-tainted (sāsrava) as its object; this is the sphere of conventional knowledge (saṃvṛtijñāna).
The path of the desire realm is the sphere of dharma-knowledge (dharmajñāna), and the path of the form realm is the sphere of subsequent knowledge (anvayajñāna).
Regarding the two knowledges of exhaustion and non-arising: these are the two knowledges of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*):
the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*).

Having completed what was to be done therein, one attains the knowledge of one beyond training; this is the knowledge of exhaustion. One does not again perform [what remains to be done] while attaining the knowledge of one beyond training. This is the knowledge of non-arising.
This is the knowledge of non-arising; it is also the knowledge of phenomena (dharma-jñāna) and the subsequent knowledge (anvaya-jñāna).
Question:
What is the objective sphere of the knowledge of exhaustion (kṣaya-jñāna) and the knowledge of non-arising?
Answer: The objects of these two types of knowledge reside in four gates; that is, the four truths:
suffering, its origin, cessation, and the path.
The ten knowledges have already been explained; their modes of activity shall now be discussed.
Two knowledges possess sixteen modes of activity: the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*) and the subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*).
Such modes of activity, or otherwise, are what is called conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*).

Regarding the two knowledges and sixteen aspects of dharma-knowledge and subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*): the nature of dharma-knowledge consists of sixteen aspects, which are subsumed under four groups of four:
the four aspects of suffering, the four aspects of origin, the four aspects of cessation, and the four aspects of the path;
this is likewise for subsequent knowledge regarding the form and formless realms.

Regarding such practice or that which is called "equal wisdom" (*samatājñāna*): the practice of equal wisdom is subsumed within the stages of Heat (*uṣmagata*), Summits (*mūrdhan*), Patience (*kṣānti*), and the Supreme Mundane Dharmas (*laukikāgradharma*); this untainted practice (*anāsravacaryā*) is subsumed within the two truths.

The first dharma among the sixteen aspects comprises four aspects of hearing and reflection, as well as the sixteen aspects of other types of conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*), such as contemplation.

Apart from these, other forms of conventional knowledge do not possess the sixteen aspects; this refers, for example, to [the conventional knowledge of] generosity, morality, loving-kindness, and so forth.
The four knowledges have four aspects, as taught in the *Niyatacaryā-śāstra*.
Regarding the knowledge of others' minds through correct contemplation, this may be either so or not so.

As for "the four knowledges have four aspects, as taught in the *Niyatacaryā-śāstra*": the knowledge of suffering has four aspects as explained above; the knowledges of origin, cessation, and the path are likewise.

Regarding the correct contemplation of the knowledge of others' minds—whether it be "this" or "not this"—the untainted (*anāsrava*) knowledge of others' minds possesses four aspects (*ākāra*) like the knowledge of the path (*mārgajñāna*); the tainted (*sāsrava*) does not.
The knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*) exclude the aspects of emptiness (*śūnyatā*) and selflessness (*anātman*);
they are said to possess fourteen aspects, with the aspect of "receiving" (*vedita*) being the most preeminent.

Regarding the statement that the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*) consist of fourteen aspects apart from the aspects of emptiness (*śūnyatā*) and selflessness (*anātman*): the knowledge of exhaustion and the knowledge of non-arising comprise fourteen aspects, excluding the aspects of emptiness and selflessness.

Why is this so? Because those practices that constitute the truths have already been performed by me and are not to be performed again; those who are empty and selfless do not engage in these practices.

Regarding the characteristic of feeling as supreme, it is not the case that all untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna*) resides within the sixteen aspects (*ṣoḍaśākāra*); rather, the sixteen aspects are the comprehensive practice.

Furthermore, there is untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna*) that experiences the sixteen aspects (*ṣoḍaśākāra*). For example, the mindfulness of the body (*kāyasmṛtyupasthāna*) is a wisdom of specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇajñāna*); it does not experience the sixteen aspects prior to being present within the sixteen applications (*ṣoḍaśākāra-prayoga*). Because this wisdom of specific characteristics experiences [the aspects] prior to all other untainted wisdoms, it is superior.
The sixteen aspects have already been explained; the knowledge attained through them shall now be discussed.
Regarding the first untainted mind, one may possess one, two, or three [aspects]; in those that follow, one aspect is added.

Regarding "the first untainted mind may be endowed with one": the first untainted mind is associated with the patience regarding the dharma of suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-kṣānti*). One who has not yet abandoned desire is endowed with one conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*), while one who has already abandoned desire is endowed with the knowledge of others' minds (*para-citta-jñāna*).

Regarding "two or three are accomplished": the second untainted mind, which is associated with the dharma-knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-jñāna*), accomplishes three knowledges—dharma-knowledge, suffering-knowledge, and conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*)—if one has not yet abandoned desire;
if one has already abandoned desire, it accomplishes the knowledge of others' minds (*paracitta-jñāna*).

Regarding the addition of one more above: among the four aforementioned occasions, one further instance is added. During these four occasions, one attains the knowledge of the unknown (*anvaya-jñāna*) upon attaining the knowledge of the suffering of the higher realms; one attains the knowledge of origination (*samudaya-jñāna*) upon attaining the dharma-knowledge of origination; one attains the knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-jñāna*) upon attaining the dharma-knowledge of cessation; and one attains the knowledge of the path (*mārga-jñāna*) upon attaining the dharma-knowledge of the path. Within the moments of receptivity (*kṣānti*), knowledge is not attained.
Question:
By which stage (bhūmi) is this wisdom subsumed? Answer:
The nine knowledges taught by the Noble Ones rely upon the higher stages;
within the dhyānas there are ten knowledges, and within the formless stages there are eight.

Regarding "the nine knowledges taught by the Noble Ones rely upon the higher stages": the preparatory dhyāna (*anāgamya*) and the intermediate dhyāna (*dhyānāntara*) lack the knowledge of others' minds, because they are subsumed under the fundamental dhyānas.
Regarding "there are ten knowledges within dhyāna," this means that within the four fundamental dhyānas there are ten knowledges.

Regarding "eight within the formless stages," this means that within the formless realms there are eight knowledges, excluding the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*) and the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*).
The sphere of the knowledge of phenomena (dharmajñāna) is the desire realm; it does not have the formless realm as its sphere.
The activity of the knowledge of others' minds (paracittajñāna) within the desire realm operates by means of the form and formless realms, yet it is itself formless.
The stages have already been explained; their cultivation shall now be discussed.
There are two kinds of cultivation:
cultivation by acquisition and cultivation by practice.

Regarding "cultivation through attainment" (*pratilambhabhāvanā*): it refers to the attainment of merits never before attained; once attained, all other merits that depend upon them are also attained, and after they have been attained, they arise spontaneously at a later time without being sought.
Regarding "the practitioner of cultivation" (*caryā-bhāvanā*): this refers to those who have previously attained meritorious qualities and now manifest them in the present.
Question:
How are these various knowledges (*jñāna*) cultivated?
Answer: If attainment is considered cultivation, this is the view of the wise and the noble ones;
that [attainment] is itself future cultivation, and the same applies to the various patiences.

Regarding those who have already attained [the knowledges] for the sake of cultivation, the noble ones perceive that these are precisely what will be cultivated in the future; within the path of seeing the truths (*darśanamārga*), they perceive that knowledge is being cultivated as it manifests in the present, namely, from the dharma-knowledge (*dharmajñāna*) up to the path-knowledge (*mārgajñāna*), which is what will be cultivated in the future.

Regarding the statement "all patiences are likewise," patience is also like this: when the *duḥkhe-dharma-jñāna-kṣānti* (receptivity to the knowledge of the dharma regarding suffering) is present before one, it is cultivated; that same *duḥkhe-dharma-jñāna-kṣānti* is what will be cultivated in the future. It is not wisdom (*jñāna*), nor is it any other patience; all cases are like this.

Regarding the statement, "In these three moments of mind, one attains the cultivation of conventional knowledge (saṃvṛti-jñāna), either seven or six [types] being cultivated; this is what is taught concerning the final moment of mind":
this means that within the path of seeing the truths (darśana-mārga), during those three moments of mind, one must cultivate conventional knowledge for the sake of the future.

Regarding the subsequent knowledge of suffering, the subsequent knowledge of origination, and the subsequent knowledge of cessation: when practicing these three truths, one attains the cultivation of conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*). Why is this so?

Having practiced these three truths, one contemplates that which is not the Truth of the Path; this refers to the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*) of those respective stages, as well as the conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*) of those stages and the desire realm.

Regarding the statement that "either seven or six [knowledges] are cultivated in the final mind": when one who is free from desire cultivates the Knowledge of the Unknown regarding the Path (*mārgānvayajñāna*), they cultivate seven knowledges, namely those comprised within the fruit of the Non-returner (*anāgāmiphala*).

One who has not yet abandoned desire cultivates six knowledges, excluding the knowledge of others' minds; because one attains the fruit of śrāmaṇya therein through the path of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, conventional knowledge is not cultivated.

Regarding the statement, "In the seventeenth untainted mind, during the subsequent path of cultivation, one should know that seven [knowledges] are cultivated; six are cultivated for the increase of the faculties":

As for "in the seventeenth untainted mind, during the subsequent path of cultivation, one should know that seven [knowledges] are cultivated," this refers to the subsequent path of cultivation following the fruit of *srotāpanna*. During these seventeen moments of mind, seven knowledges must be cultivated. Since this path is subsumed under the *anāgāmya* (future) dhyāna, there is no knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*) therein.

The knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*) belong to those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*); for this reason, the remaining seven knowledges must necessarily be cultivated. Why is this so?

Because the mind of such a person is never empty of these virtues. If one were not to cultivate them, having once attained them and then lost them, and not yet attained them again, the mind would be empty during that interval; yet it is not empty. Therefore, they must necessarily be cultivated.

Regarding the six types of increasing the faculties (*indriya-vardhana*): "increasing the faculties" refers to one liberated by faith (*śraddhādhimukta*) who increases their faculties and attains the state of one who has attained vision (*dṛṣṭiprāpta*).

Such a person possesses nine paths of non-obstruction (*ānantarya-mārga*) and nine paths of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*), and in all these paths of non-obstruction and paths of liberation, they cultivate the six knowledges (*jñāna*).
This teaching refers to one who has not yet abandoned desire; therefore, such a person lacks the knowledge of others' minds.

At that time, while training in the path, they do not train in the severance of afflictions; since they have never before attained the cultivation of merit nor previously acquired it, they do not cultivate conventional knowledge (*samvṛti-jñāna*).
When attaining the fruit of non-returning (anāgāmiphala), one is far removed from the seven stages;
contemplating and training in the various supernormal powers (abhijñā), one practices eight liberations.

Regarding "when attaining the fruit of non-returning": if one attains the fruit of non-returning and cultivates the eight knowledges (jñāna), therein one must necessarily attain the fundamental dhyānas (mauladhyāna). For this reason, one cultivates the knowledge of others' minds (paracittajñāna); the remaining knowledges are as previously described.

Regarding "being far removed from the seventh stage": when one becomes detached from the four dhyānas and the three formless attainments, one cultivates the eight knowledges (*jñāna*) throughout all nine paths of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*); therein, one cultivates all the meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*) of the lower stages.
Regarding the "eight [knowledges] cultivated through the three supernormal powers, the path of liberation, and the practice":

the three supernormal powers are the bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*), the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*), and the divine ear (*divyaśrotra*); in all nine paths of liberation (*vimuktimārga*), one cultivates eight knowledges (*jñāna*).
Why is this? Because it encompasses the fundamental dhyānas.
Within this path of non-obstruction, one also extinguishes the state of the peak of existence (bhavāgra).
Regarding those eight paths of liberation, it is said that seven are cultivated.

At the time of becoming free from desire in the seven stages, one cultivates seven knowledges within all the paths of non-obstruction (*ānantarya-mārga*), excluding the knowledge of others' minds (*paracitta-jñāna*).

Why is this? Because this path of non-obstruction cultivates the knowledge of the destruction of fetters (*saṃyojana-kṣaya-jñāna*), whereas the knowledge of others' minds (*paracitta-jñāna*) does not destroy fetters; therefore, it is not cultivated.

Regarding the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*), the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, when one becomes detached from it, one cultivates seven knowledges within the eight paths of liberation, excluding conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*).
Why is this so? Because conventional knowledge (*samvṛti-jñāna*) turns back at the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, as it does not transcend it.
To transcend the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*), there are six cultivations of the path of non-obstruction (*anantarya-mārga*).
One should know that when ascending, one cultivates the lower stages.

Regarding the six types of knowledge cultivated during the path of non-obstruction (*ānantarya-mārga*) for those detached from the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*): at the time of becoming detached from the first dhyāna, one cultivates six types of knowledge within the nine paths of non-obstruction, excluding the knowledge of others' minds (*paracitta-jñāna*) and conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*).

Regarding the statement that one who rides upon a higher stage should know how to cultivate the lower stages: it should be understood that this cultivation of all stages involves cultivating the various knowledges of one's own stage as well as those subsumed under the lower stages.

That is to say, based on the detachment from desire through the first dhyāna, one cultivates the meritorious qualities of two stages: those comprised within one's own stage and those of the "future" dhyāna (anāgāmya); and so it continues up to the sphere of nothingness.
"All outflows and the outflow-free, the merits cultivated across all stages, within the initial mind of one beyond training—this is the intention of 'subsequent knowledge' (anvaya-jñāna).

Regarding "all outflows and the outflow-free, the merits cultivated across all stages, within the initial mind of one beyond training": at the moment of attaining the fruit of Arhatship (the state of being unattached), the merits cultivated throughout the nine stages as well as one's own stage—and indeed across all stages—are attained therein.
Why is this so? Because it is contrary to the afflictions of the stage of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
In all stages, the mind accompanied by afflictions is not clear and pure; the mind free from afflictions is clear and pure. Therefore, one abandons those [afflictions] and cultivates everything.
Question:
With what wisdom is this initial mind of one beyond training associated? Answer:
This is the mind of the knowledge of what is yet to be known; it is the first mind of one beyond training (aśaikṣa) associated with the knowledge of what is yet to be known.
He forms this thought:
"Birth has been extinguished for me."
This is the condition for birth in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception. Why is this?
Because it is the ultimate end.
Therefore, it is associated with the "knowledge of the unknown regarding suffering" (*duḥkhe 'jñāsyāmīti-jñāna*).
Question:
Furthermore, the Blessed One spoke of vision (*darśana*), knowledge (*jñāna*), and wisdom (*prajñā*); are these three of one kind or of different kinds?
Answer:

This is a differentiation of wisdom; it is the very nature of wisdom, yet because of its specific objects, the Blessed One sometimes calls it "view" (dṛṣṭi) and sometimes calls it "knowledge" (jñāna).
Question:
What is the meaning of this?
The answer is:
It refers to the definitive knowledge that all types of patience (kṣānti) do not possess the nature of wisdom (jñāna).
The knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) is not a vision (*darśana*); the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*) is likewise so.

As for the claim that the various patiences (*kṣānti*) definitely know their objects but are not of the nature of knowledge: because one cultivates the eight patiences in order to seek [the truths], they are vision because they can see, and wisdom (*prajñā*) because they can discern; however, they are not knowledge, because they are not yet definitive.
Why is this? It is because it functions as an initial condition (*pratyaya*).

As for the statement that "the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) is not vision (*darśana*), and the same applies to the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*)," the knowledge of exhaustion and the knowledge of non-arising are wisdom (*prajñā*) by virtue of seeing and knowledge (*jñāna*) by virtue of being determinate; however, they are not vision, because they do not seek and have no further objective to accomplish.
The remaining types of untainted wisdom consist of all three natures:
vision, knowledge, and discernment.
Wholesome mundane tainted knowledge resides in the mind and in the various views.
One should know that this is "view"; it is said that all [such] is wisdom (*prajñā*).

Regarding the statement, "Wholesome mundane contaminated wisdom (*sāsrava-kuśala-prajñā*) belonging to the mind and various views—one should know that this is 'view'": within the stage of the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna-bhūmi*), wholesome contaminated wisdom consists of three natures:
view, knowledge, and wisdom.
