The five views are of the nature of affliction because they possess the quality of observation;
furthermore, they are not separate from knowledge (*jñāna*) and wisdom (*prajñā*).
Other types of tainted wisdom (*sāsravā prajñā*) do not possess the nature of view.
Why is this so? The seeds of wisdom associated with the indeterminate mental consciousness do not possess the nature of vision (*dṛṣṭi*), because they lack investigative discernment.
Furthermore, the seeds of defiled wisdom also do not possess the nature of vision, because they are corrupted by the afflictions (*kleśa*).
The seeds of wisdom associated with the five consciousnesses are also not of the nature of vision (*darśana*), because they lack investigative observation;
yet they are also not devoid of the nature of knowledge (*jñāna*).

When it is said that all [these] are wisdom, this refers to the exclusions previously mentioned: just as within patience (*kṣānti*) there is the exclusion of knowledge, so too do the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*) exclude vision.
Excluding the level of wholesome mental consciousness and the five views, the remaining contaminated wisdom is dissociated from view.
Wisdom is not like this. Why is that?
Because the seeds of all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*) and the seeds of all-seeing (*sarvadarśitā*) are themselves the seeds of wisdom (*prajñā*).
Question: How many objects of knowledge do each of these knowledges take as their cognitive objects?
Answer: Dharma-knowledge and subsequent knowledge (anvaya-jñāna) clearly comprehend nine knowledges;
causal knowledge and resultant knowledge are the objects of these two knowledges.

Regarding the statement that "dharma-knowledge and subsequent knowledge (anvaya-jñāna) clearly comprehend nine knowledges": dharma-knowledge contemplates nine knowledges and takes nine knowledges as its object, excluding subsequent knowledge. Why is this so?
The knowledge of the unknown (anājñāta-ājñāna) is not the fruit of the desire realm, nor the cause of the desire realm, nor the cessation of the desire realm, nor the path of the desire realm.
The knowledge of the unknown is likewise [not the object of] nine knowledges, excluding the knowledge of phenomena (dharma-jñāna).

Regarding the statement that "the knowledge of causes and the knowledge of results are the objects of these two knowledges": the knowledge of cultivation (*bhāvanājñāna*) is the knowledge of causes; this is because the contaminated knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*) and the conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*) take cultivation as their common object. The others do not take it as an object, because they are uncontaminated (*anāsrava*).
The knowledge of suffering is likewise; this is the knowledge of the fruit.
The knowledge of the path consists of nine knowledges. The knowledge of liberation has no object;
it is said by the One of Certain Wisdom to have all things as its domain.

Regarding the statement that "the knowledge of the path consists of nine knowledges": the objective sphere of the knowledge of the path comprises nine knowledges; it does not take conventional knowledge as its object because conventional knowledge is outflowing (sāsrava).
All others take it as their object, because they share the same truth of the path.

Regarding "the knowledge of liberation has no object": the knowledge of liberation is the knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-jñāna*), not the knowledge of objects (*ālambana-jñāna*), because it takes the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) as its object.
Regarding "all other spheres are what is taught by the knowledge of determination": there are four other knowledges that take all ten knowledges as their objects.
Conventional knowledge (*samvṛti-jñāna*) takes ten knowledges as its objects, because its sphere consists of all phenomena (*sarva-dharma*).
Knowledge of others' minds (*paracitta-jñāna*) also takes ten knowledges as its objects, because it possesses the sphere of others' minds.

Knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣaya-jñāna*) and knowledge of non-arising (*anutpāda-jñāna*) also take ten knowledges as their objects, because their sphere consists of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*).
Question:

Furthermore, the Blessed One said that one attains the fruit of non-attachment by means of the knowledge of the unknown (*anājñāta-ājñāna-jñāna*), as if departing from the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*).
This knowledge of the unknown is the path to that [fruit]; it cannot be known by means of this [other knowledge].
Is it only the knowledge of the unknown (anvaya-jñāna) that is the path for those [realms], and not others? Answer:
There is also the knowledge of phenomena (dharma-jñāna) that serves as the path for the form and formless realms.
Question:
Which ones? Answer:
If cessation and the path are the domain of the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*), they bring about the extinction of the three realms;
this is not the case for the subsequent knowledge of desire (*anvayajñāna*).

If cessation and the path are the domain of the knowledge of phenomena and bring about the extinction of the three realms, this refers to the knowledge of phenomena regarding cessation (*nirodhadharmajñāna*) and the knowledge of phenomena regarding the path (*mārgadharmajñāna*); within the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), these extinguish the fetters of the three realms.

There may be a dharma-knowledge that is free from desire for the form and formless realms; that is, one who views this [desire] as particularly grave and evil, and thus contemplates cessation and the path regarding the desire realm.
This is freedom from desire for the form and formless realms, yet it is neither the knowledge of suffering nor the knowledge of origination.
Why is this? Because they do not share the same suffering or its origin, but share the same cessation and path.
Question:
Is there any "knowledge of the unknown" (*anājñātam-ājñāsyāmī-jñāna*) that ceases the desire realm?
Answer: No;
the knowledge of the unknown does not [cease] desire.
There is no faculty of "I-shall-come-to-know-the-unknown" that can extinguish [defilements] in the desire realm. Why is this?
Because there is no such heavy view of evil other than this.
Question:
Regarding the nature of the supernormal knowledges (*abhijñā*), it should also be stated how many knowledges each one possesses. Answer:
The knowledge of the bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*) and so forth, as well as the divine eye and ear, are likewise [conventional].
Regarding the six [knowledges] concerning past lives, five are said to be the knowledge of others' minds.

As for "the knowledge of the bases of psychic power and so forth, as well as the divine eye and ear, are likewise": the bases of psychic power are explained as conventional knowledge; the divine eye and divine ear are also thus. Untainted knowledge (*anāsrava-jñāna*) does not proceed by means of these.
Regarding the six [knowledges] concerning past lives (*pūrvanivāsa*): the supernormal power of recollecting past lives consists of six knowledges.

The knowledge of phenomena (*dharma-jñāna*) recollects the portion of the knowledge of phenomena; the knowledge of the unknown (*anvaya-jñāna*) recollects the portion of the knowledge of the unknown; conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*) recollects the conventional; the knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-jñāna*) recollects the past; the knowledge of the origin of suffering (*samudaya-jñāna*) recollects the past origin; and the knowledge of the path (*mārga-jñāna*) recollects the past path.
Regarding the fifth, the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*): the supernormal power of knowing others' minds consists of five types of knowledge.
The knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*) knows the *dharmajñāna* within another's mind, as well as the primary mind and its associated mental factors (*caitta-dharma*) that are associated with it;
the subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*) is likewise.
Conventional knowledge (saṃvṛti-jñāna) knows the mundane minds and mental factors of others;
path-knowledge (mārga-jñāna) knows the untainted minds and mental factors of others; and the knowledge of others' minds (paracitta-jñāna) comprises five [types].
These nine knowledges constitute the supernormal power of the exhaustion of outflows (āsravakṣaya-abhijñā), as taught by the Noble One.
The eight objects pertain to the body; the Dharma [object] pertains to nineteen [factors] and two knowledges.

Regarding the "nine knowledges" mentioned by the Noble Ones as the supernormal power of the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya-abhijñā*): this supernormal power consists of nine untainted (*anāsrava*) knowledges, because it is diametrically opposed to all outflows.
Question:
Furthermore, the Blessed One said that the application of mindfulness which consists in contemplating the body as body is wisdom (*prajñā*).
To which type of knowledge does this application of mindfulness belong?
Answer:

Regarding the eight objects within the body, the eight knowledges observe the bodily form as a conventional designation of "body"; these are known by the eight knowledges, excluding the knowledge of others' minds and the knowledge of cessation.
If wisdom takes form (*rūpa*) as its object, it is the application of mindfulness to the body (*kāyasmṛtyupasthāna*);

these two types of wisdom do not take form as their object. Regarding the ten [types of] phenomena (*dharma*): the application of mindfulness to phenomena (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*) possesses ten types of wisdom. Excluding form, sensation (*vedanā*), and mind (*citta*), the remaining phenomena are called "phenomena. These objects consist of the ten types of wisdom regarding specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) and realms (*dhātu*), as well as the universal (*sarvatraga*). Such is the application of mindfulness to phenomena.
Regarding "nine knowledges in two": the nine knowledges associated with sensation and mind exclude the knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-jñāna*).

That is to say, when knowledge takes sensation as its object, it is the application of mindfulness to sensation; when knowledge takes the mind as its object, it is the application of mindfulness to the mind.
Question:
All Tathāgatas possess the power of knowledge (*jñānabala*). How is the Tathāgata’s power established as knowledge?
Furthermore, regarding the nature of the four fearlessnesses (*vaiśāradya*) possessed by the Tathāgata, how is it that he declares, "I am perfectly awakened"?
Regarding these phenomena, before attaining equal and perfect enlightenment, one does not perceive their characteristics.
In this same manner, all of these should also be analyzed: for each one, how many types of knowledge constitute its nature?
Answer:
The power of the possible and the impossible, as well as the foremost fearlessness—these constitute the ten knowledges of a Buddha; the others are distinctions within these.

Regarding "the power of the possible and the impossible (*sthānāsthāna-bala*) and the fearlessnesses are foremost; these are the ten knowledges of a Buddha": the Buddha possesses ten knowledges. The power of the possible and the impossible is the name for the knowledge of what is possible. It refers to receiving the true characteristics and true modes of all phenomena, and receiving the knowledge that such phenomena have such characteristics and such modes. This is called the knowledge of the possible and the knowledge of the impossible.

When one realizes that in all phenomena the characteristics and activities of others are unattainable, then one knows that these phenomena do not possess such characteristics or such activities; this is called the knowledge of the impossible.
These are the ten knowledges (*jñāna*) of a Buddha; the first fearlessness (*vaiśāradya*) likewise consists of ten knowledges because it is an equal and perfect attainment (*samāpatti*).

As for the other distinctions within this context: the power regarding what is possible and impossible (*sthānāsthāna-bala*) is differentiated into the ten powers, while the first fearlessness is differentiated into the four grounds of self-confidence (*vaiśāradya*). Because the knowledge of what is possible and impossible is a distinction of objective spheres (*viṣaya*), it is analyzed into ten types.
The first fearlessness also involves a distinction of its objects; therefore, it is analyzed into four types.
Question:
Since the four analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*) are also of the nature of wisdom, they too should be analyzed: how many wisdoms does each one consist of?

Answer: The analytical knowledge of phenomena (dharma-pratisaṃvid) and the analytical knowledge of expression (nirukti-pratisaṃvid) are one; the analytical knowledge of meaning (artha-pratisaṃvid) and the analytical knowledge of eloquence (pratibhāna-pratisaṃvid) each consist of ten.
The knowledge resulting from prayer (praṇidhi-jñāna) consists of seven knowledges; this is what was taught by the Most Victorious One (Jinavara).

Regarding the first pair, the discrimination of dharmas (*dharma-pratisaṃvid*) and the discrimination of eloquence (*nirukti-pratisaṃvid*): "discrimination of dharmas" refers to the awakening to all phenomena. This is designated as conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*), not by way of receiving its name from untainted knowledge (*anāsrava-jñāna*).
Within the conventional world, names are mere designations; untainted knowledge does not function by means of these.
The analytical knowledge of eloquence (*pratibhāna-pratisaṃvid*) is called "correct teaching"; this is also conventional wisdom (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*), a provisional designation within the mundane realm.

Regarding the statement that the analytical knowledge of meaning (*artha-pratisaṃvid*) is associated with ten [knowledges]: the analytical knowledge of meaning is called "contemplation" (*vipaśyanā*) and "manifestation" (*abhimukhībhāva*); it consists of the ten knowledges as a skillful means (*upāya-jñāna*) that is unimpeded.

The analytical knowledge of meaning (*arthapratibhāna*) is defined as awakening to the true reality of all phenomena; it likewise consists of the ten knowledges, because it apprehends their true characteristics. As for the person [who speaks], it is said that there are two types of analytical eloquence (*pratibhāna*):

first, the analytical eloquence of language (*niruktipratibhāna*), which corresponds to conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*); second, the analytical eloquence of dharma and meaning (*dharmārthapratibhāna*), which corresponds to the ten knowledges.
Question:
How many knowledges does the knowledge of aspiration (praṇidhijñāna) comprise? Answer:
The knowledge of aspiration consists of seven knowledges; this is what was taught by the Most Victorious One.
The knowledge of aspiration comprises seven knowledges, excluding the knowledge of others' minds, the knowledge of exhaustion, and the knowledge of non-arising.
The knowledge of vows has a swift and nimble range; it receives all dharmas throughout the three periods of time. This is the nature of the seven knowledges. Those who possess it say:
first, the knowledge of equality.
7. Chapter on Concentration (Samādhi-varga). Question:
Having thus understood these various knowledges, how should this knowledge be described? Answer:
Wisdom relies upon the various meditative concentrations (*samādhi*) to practice unimpeded conduct;
therefore, one contemplates concentration in order to seek its true reality.
When wisdom relies upon the various meditative concentrations to practice unimpeded conduct, it is like a lamp relying on oil: in a place sheltered from the wind, its flame is exceedingly bright.

In this way, wisdom relies upon meditative concentration; when the mind is free from all distractions, the light of wisdom becomes exceedingly bright, and one proceeds toward the object of focus with certainty and without doubt.
Therefore, by contemplating concentration, one seeks its true reality.
It is definitively taught that there are the four dhyānas and the formless attainments;
each of these is explained as being of mixed, flavoring, pure, and untainted types.
Regarding the definitive teaching of the four dhyānas and the formless attainments, there are eight meditative absorptions (samāpatti).

Regarding the four dhyānas and the four formless attainments (*ārūpya-samāpatti*), each one within these is described as being associated with the "taste" (*āsvāda*), the "pure" (*śuddha*), and the "outflow-free" (*anāsrava*). Specifically, the first dhyāna has three types:
that which is associated with taste, the pure, and the outflow-free.
Regarding all such doors of concentration (*samādhimukha*),
how are they associated with relish (*āsvāda-saṃprayukta*)?
How are they pure (*śuddha*)?
What is the untainted? Answer:
That which is wholesome and tainted is "pure"; that which is without fever is called "untainted."
The flavors of craving are associated with attachment; the supreme state is the untainted (anāsrava).
When it is said that "the wholesome tainted is pure," it means that because the wholesome is pure, it is therefore called pure.

"Without fever" refers to that which is untainted (*anāsrava*); "fever" is a metaphorical designation for the afflictions (*kleśa*), meaning that what is definitively free from afflictions is untainted.

"Associated with the relish of flavor" refers to being associated with craving for the meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*) and the formless attainments (*ārūpyasamāpatti*); this constitutes being fully endowed with, and proceeding together with, such association, which is called "associated with relish."

Regarding "the supreme is without outflows": the supreme [state] is the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*); therein there are no outflows, because it does not proceed with rapid movement.
This consists of three types, and each of the others likewise consists of three types.
Question:
Of what nature is dhyāna? Answer:
Having five factors with applied and sustained thought, And likewise possessing three feelings, With various kinds of fourfold mind— This is called the first dhyāna.
As for the "five factors," they refer to the five factors that sustain the first dhyāna and make it firm; it is also from these that the name is derived.
Vitarka (applied thought), vicāra (sustained thought), prīti (joy), sukha (bliss), and ekāgratā (one-pointedness of mind).
Vitarka refers to the arising of wholesome merit at the time of entering meditative concentration; it is the initial coarse mental reflection.
Vicāra refers to causing the mind to become subtle, continuous, and connected.
Joy (*prīti*) is defined as gladness within meditative concentration.
Pleasure (*sukha*) is defined as the physical and mental well-being and happiness resulting from that gladness.
One-pointedness of mind (*ekāgratā*) is defined as the mind being focused exclusively on its object without distraction.
This type [of dhyāna] has these factors as its branches during the time of abiding in concentration, as well as at the time of entry and the time of relinquishing; therefore, it has five branches.
Regarding the first dhyāna having vitarka and vicāra: that which possesses vitarka and vicāra is precisely the first dhyāna.
Question:
Since one has already attained the five factors [of dhyāna], what further use is there for vitarka and vicāra? Answer:

"Branches" refers to the wholesome; however, among the five branches, it is taught that there are those which are defiled or neutral, as well as those characterized by both initial application (*vitarka*) and sustained application (*vicāra*) that are not wholesome.
Furthermore, regarding "there are also three feelings," the first dhyāna possesses three feelings:
the faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*), the faculty of joy (*saumanasyendriya*), and the faculty of equanimity (*upekṣendriya*).

Among the sensations, the faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*) pertains to bodily sensation; the faculty of joy (*saumanasyendriya*) belongs to the mental level (*manobhūmi*); and the faculty of equanimity (*upekṣendriya*) resides in the four consciousnesses.
As for "of various kinds," this refers to the various kinds within the Brahma-world, which have higher and lower levels; this is called the complete birth-place.
Regarding the four minds: the first dhyāna has four minds—eye-consciousness, ear-consciousness, body-consciousness, and mind-consciousness.
That which is called "this is the first dhyāna" refers to all these dharmas as being the first dhyāna.
The first dhyāna has already been explained; the second shall now be discussed.
There are two types of sensation, and the second dhyāna has four factors;
the third has five factors, and this dhyāna is said to have two sensations.
Regarding "two feelings": in the second dhyāna there are two feelings—the faculty of joy (*prīti-indriya*) and the faculty of equanimity (*upekṣā-indriya*).

Regarding "of various kinds": within that state, the body is of various kinds; having already abandoned applied and sustained thought (*vitarka-vicāra*), the mind is of various kinds, sometimes entering the faculty of joy and sometimes entering the faculty of equanimity; however, joy is the fundamental [feeling], while the faculty of equanimity exists at its periphery.

Regarding the four factors of the second dhyāna: the second dhyāna has four factors—inner serenity (*adhyātmasaṃprasāda*), joy (*prīti*), bliss (*sukha*), and one-pointedness of mind (*cittaikāgratā*).
Inner serenity is another name for faith; it is the faith that arises within the state of detachment.
Having attained detachment through the first dhyāna, one then reflects:
"All things are to be detached from.
The remaining factors are as previously explained.
This factor is a limb of the second dhyāna.
There are five limbs in the third; the third dhyāna has five limbs:
bliss, equanimity, mindfulness, wisdom, and one-pointedness of mind.
"Joy" (*sukha*) refers to the faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*) within the sphere of mental consciousness (*manovijñāna-bhūmi*).
"Guarding" (*upekṣā*) refers to one who, having already experienced joy, does not seek anything further; as it is said:
"Although 'guarding' has its own meaning, it should not be called a 'limb' [of dhyāna]. "Mindfulness" (*smṛti*) is the non-abandonment of the means for guarding.
Wisdom does not cause [the mind] to delight;
one-pointedness is concentration.
This factor is a limb within the third dhyāna.
Regarding the statement that this dhyāna has two types of sensation (*vedanā*):

in the third dhyāna there are two sensations, namely the faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*) and the faculty of equanimity (*upekṣendriya*). The faculty of pleasure is the fundamental [sensation], while the faculty of equanimity is the derivative.
Free from inhalation and exhalation, the fourth [dhyāna] possesses four factors;
these factors are said to be wholesome and are further distinguished by their types.
"Free from inhalation and exhalation" means that inhalation is coming and exhalation is going, both of which are absent within the fourth dhyāna.
Why is this so? Because by virtue of the power of meditative concentration (*samādhi*), the pores of his body close.
Regarding "the fourth has four factors": the fourth dhyāna possesses four factors.
Neither-painful-nor-pleasant, equanimity, pure mindfulness, and one-pointedness of mind.
Seeking freedom from pain and pleasure, there is neither-pain-nor-pleasure;
the rest is as previously explained.
Question:
Which dhyāna is associated with the factors (aṅga)? Answer:
These factors are said to be wholesome.
Being associated with the wholesome factors of dhyāna, they are neither defiled nor indeterminate.

Furthermore, regarding the classification of their seeds: since the seeds have already been explained according to their respective locations, it should be understood that they cannot exist in other locations.
Just as the first dhyāna possesses vitarka and vicāra, these types are said to exist in four states of mind, but they are absent in all other stages.
Since the fourth dhyāna is free from inhalation and exhalation, these three [types] are absent therein and should not be mentioned.
The four dhyānas and the four formless attainments have already been explained; as for the remainder, they shall now be discussed.
Question:
As the Blessed One said, there is a fundamental basis [for these states] even for one who has not yet abandoned desire.
There are no untainted (*anāsrava*) merits without a fundamental basis.
To which stage (*bhūmi*) are these untainted merits subsumed? Answer:
It is subsumed within the future dhyāna.
Furthermore, the Blessed One has spoken of three concentrations:
with vitarka and vicāra, without vitarka and with subtle vicāra, and without vitarka and without vicāra.
Among these, the first dhyāna possesses both vitarka (applied thought) and vicāra (sustained thought), while the second dhyāna is without vitarka and without vicāra.
As for the concentration that is without vitarka but possesses slight vicāra, to which stage does it belong?
Answer: It is comprised within the intermediate dhyāna.
I shall now explain the characteristics of this future dhyāna and the intermediate dhyāna.
"Associated with vitarka and vicāra, both are present in the preliminary dhyāna (anāgamya-dhyāna);
associated with vicāra alone, it is in the intermediate [dhyāna]; this is what the wise have taught.
Regarding "associated with vitarka and vicāra, both are present in the preliminary dhyāna": within the preliminary dhyāna, there is both vitarka and vicāra.

Regarding what is taught by the One of Clear Wisdom concerning the intermediate state associated with observation (*vipaśyanā*): in the intermediate dhyāna there is little observation and no initial application (*vitarka*); therein the mind gradually comes to rest.
It is independent and of two kinds; excluding that which is associated with relish (*āsvādita*), the intermediate dhyāna has three types, all of which are said to possess a single feeling (*vedanā*).

Regarding the two types that are without support and exclude those associated with flavor (*sāsvāda*): future dhyāna is exclusively wholesome, being both contaminated (*sāsrava*) and uncontaminated (*anāsrava*). The contaminated is "pure" (*śubha*), while the uncontaminated is simply "uncontaminated."
Regarding "there are three kinds of intermediate dhyāna," there are three types of intermediate dhyāna:
the tainted (*sāsrava*), the pure (*śuddha*), and the untainted (*anāsrava*); this is because it is a dwelling place for birth and death.

As for the statement that "both are said to have one feeling," both the preparatory dhyāna (*anāgamya*) and the intermediate dhyāna possess the faculty of equanimity as their single feeling, because they are not fundamental stages (*maulabhūmi*).
Having already explained the various qualities associated with the meditative absorptions (*samāpatti*), I shall now explain how they are subsumed therein.
The meditative concentrations (*samādhi*) possess supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), the immeasurables (*apramāṇa*), the cultivation of all things,
the bases of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*), the knowledges (*jñāna*), and the liberations (*vimokṣa*) arise within them.
Regarding samādhi, there are three samādhis:
emptiness, wishlessness, and signlessness, because the untainted mind is bound [to them].
Regarding the supernormal powers, there are six supernormal powers:

The knowledge of the bases of psychic power, the knowledge of the divine ear, the knowledge of the supernormal power of reading others' minds, the knowledge of recollecting past lives, the knowledge of death and rebirth, and the knowledge of the supernormal power of the exhaustion of outflows.
As for the immeasurables, there are four immeasurables:
loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity.
Because it is the sphere of immeasurable sentient beings, it is called "immeasurable.
Regarding the cultivation of all things, there are the ten totalities (*kṛtsnāyatana*):

the totality of earth, the totalities of water, fire, wind, blue, yellow, red, and white, the totality of the base of infinite space, and the totality of the base of infinite consciousness; they are called "totalities" because one fully possesses and understands them all.
Regarding the spheres of liberation (*vimokṣa*), there are eight spheres of liberation:

(1) internally not yet having removed the perception of form, one contemplates the impure with a limited object; (2) [internally not yet having removed the perception of form,] one contemplates the impure with an immeasurable object; (3) having removed the perception of form, one contemplates the impure with a limited object; (4) having removed the perception of form, one contemplates the impure with an immeasurable object; and furthermore, the spheres of liberation consisting of the contemplation of blue, yellow, red, and white, having removed the perception of form.
Because they eliminate impure objects, they are called "bases of elimination" (*vibhūṣaṇāyatana*).
As for "the various knowledges," there are ten such knowledges, as previously explained.
Regarding "liberations," there are eight liberations (*aṣṭavimokṣa*):

First, the contemplation of impurity while not yet having eliminated the perception of form; second, the contemplation of impurity after having eliminated the perception of form; third, the contemplation of purity; and fourth, the four formless attainments and the attainment of cessation.
Because one turns one's back on and does not face the objective realm (*viṣaya*), it is called "liberation" (*vimukti*).
Regarding those who arise therein, these various merits can be attained within the nine stages; as for the person who arises therein, it is said they should belong to the tenth stage (*daśabhūmi*).
The various virtues that may be attained according to each stage have already been explained; they shall now be set forth.
Wisdom, compassion, and protection, as well as loving-kindness and the five supernormal powers, are said to pervade all four dhyānas;
within the sixth [dhyāna], there is manifest knowledge.

Regarding the statement that "one wisdom, compassion, and protective loving-kindness, as well as the five supernormal powers, are said to pervade all four dhyānas": "one wisdom" refers to the knowledge of others' minds (paracittajñāna), the three immeasurables (apramāṇa), and the five supernormal powers (abhijñā). These are all fundamental virtues that exist within the four primary dhyānas (maula-dhyāna) and not elsewhere.

Regarding "there is manifest knowledge within the six": manifest knowledge is dharma-knowledge; it exists within six stages: the four fundamental dhyānas, the preliminary dhyāna (anāgamyadhyāna), and the intermediate dhyāna (dhyānāntara).
Within the *kṛtsnāyatana* (totalities), four are taught; among them, there is also joy (*prīti*).
The first two liberations (*vimokṣa*) possess these qualities within the first and second *dhyānas*.
The first four totalities, such as joy and the rest, as well as the first and second liberations—these qualities exist only within the first and second *dhyānas*, and not elsewhere.

The bases of mastery (abhibhvāyatana) are said to be the remaining ones, together with one liberation (vimokṣa), as well as the eight universal bases (kṛtsnāyatana); the Buddha taught these as the supreme dhyāna.
The latter four bases of mastery and the pure liberations, along with the first eight universal bases—these qualities exist within the fourth dhyāna and nowhere else.
"The remaining liberations are explained by their own names; the two 'all-encompassing' [spheres] are likewise so.
Cessation comes last; the remaining nine are said to be untainted.

Regarding "the remaining liberations are explained by their own names; the two 'all-encompassing' are likewise so": the other four liberations are explained by their respective names, and the two all-encompassing spheres (*kṛtsnāyatana*) are also thus.

The liberation of the base of infinite space, the universal base of infinite space, and that which is subsumed within the base of infinite space; thus it continues up to the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
Regarding "cessation occurs last": the attainment of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti) is subsumed under the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana).
Why is this so? Because one enters it even while not yet free from desire for that sphere.
"The remaining nine refer to those that are untainted" means that the remaining untainted dharmas are comprised within the nine stages (*bhūmi*).
For example, the three samādhis, the seven knowledges (*jñāna*), and the supernormal power of the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya-abhijñā*) are comprised within these nine stages.
The four dhyānas, the three formless attainments, the preliminary stage (anāgamyam), and the intermediate dhyāna—
these constitute the ten stages in which conventional knowledge (saṃvṛtijñāna) is subsumed.

This [conventional knowledge] is also obtainable in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana), because it is included within the fixed number of meditative stages.
Question:
Of these merits, how many are with outflows (sāsrava) and how many are without outflows (anāsrava)? Answer:
Regarding the three liberations, one should know that they are both with-outflows (*sāsrava*) and without-outflows (*anāsrava*).
Having already distinguished them as concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*), it is said that all others are entirely with-outflows.

As for "the three liberations should be known as being both with-outflows and without-outflows": the liberations of the immeasurable sphere of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*), the immeasurable sphere of infinite consciousness (*vijñānānantyāyatana*), and the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*) are both with-outflows and without-outflows.
Regarding "concentration and wisdom are non-conceptual": concentration is as explained in the *Sūtra-skandha*.
The untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna*) and the various supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) are as explained in the *Jñāna-skandha*.

As for "the remainder is entirely with outflows" (*sāsrava*): all other meritorious qualities are exclusively with outflows because they consist of the three supernormal powers and the modes of deportment (*airyāpathika*), because they have the characteristics of form, sound, and feeling, because they take immeasurable sentient beings as their object, and because they involve the mental engagement and aspiration of the spheres of totality (*kṛtsnāyatana*).

The three liberations are also like this: the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception is not a rapid movement because it is free from the cessation and departure of perception and wisdom, and because it is devoid of applied and sustained thought; furthermore, the spheres of mastery are also [liberations] because they involve mental resolve and aspiration.
The characteristics of the various merits have already been explained; their accomplishment shall now be discussed.
One who has not yet transcended desire accomplishes the meditative absorptions associated with relish (*āsvādanasamprayukta*);
one who has transcended the lower but not yet reached the higher accomplishes the pure (*śuddha*) meditative absorptions.

"Unable to transcend and having accomplished those associated with relishing" means that if one has not yet abandoned desire for a particular stage, one accomplishes the states associated with relishing within that stage.

"Having attained the lower but not yet reached the upper, one accomplishes the pure meditative absorptions" means that having abandoned the desires of the Desire Realm, if one has not yet been born in a higher stage above the Brahma World, one accomplishes the pure First Dhyāna as well as the contaminated merits belonging to the stage of the First Dhyāna.
All such things should be known in this way.
One who dwells in the higher [stages] should know that they have accomplished the untainted dhyānas and sought to attain all merits;
yet one should know that these do not exist within the state of desirelessness.

Regarding the statement that one dwelling above should be known as accomplishing the untainted (*anāsrava*) dhyānas: this means that when one dwells in a higher stage having abandoned the desires of the lower stages, one also accomplishes the untainted [dhyānas] of those lower stages.

Just as one who has seen the truths and is free from desire dwells in the Brahma-world or higher stages, accomplishing the untainted first dhyāna and all other untainted virtues such as the meditative concentrations of the first dhyāna stage.
All such cases should be understood in this way:

mundane merits are bound to the place where they arise, whereas untainted merits reside within cessation; therefore, one leaves behind the place of arising and relinquishes tainted merits, but does not relinquish the untainted.

Regarding the statement that "one attains various merits, knowing they are not [attained] within the state of being free from desire": it has already been explained that one achieves higher merits by becoming free from the desires of lower stages; however, it should be understood that not all merits are attained at the very moment of becoming free from desire.

Just as the knowledge of the bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*), the knowledge of the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*), and the knowledge of the divine ear (*divyaśrotra*) are of an indeterminate nature (*avyākṛta*), so too all desire and the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*) are sought through this; they are not attained at the time of abandoning desire for the lower stages.
The accomplishment has already been explained; the causal conditions shall now be discussed.
There are twenty-three types of meditative concentration (*samādhi*):
eight associated with the flavorful (*sāsvāda*), eight pure (*śuddha*), and seven untainted (*anāsrava*).
Question:
How many types of causes are there for each of these? Answer:
Sublime, untainted, and undefiled, the seven kinds are called causes;
regarding pure dhyāna associated with the flavor [of concentration], one should know that there is one cause.
As for "the sublime, untainted, and undefiled seven kinds are called causes," each of the untainted [dhyānas] consists of seven kinds.
The natural cause (*nisyanda-hetu*), the associated cause (*samprayukta-hetu*) of its own stage, and the universal cause (*sarvatraga-hetu*).

Regarding the statement that "for the pure [dhyāna] associated with relish, one should know that there is one cause": the first dhyāna associated with relish has as its cause only the first dhyāna associated with relish, and nothing else.
It is not the cause of wholesome states, because they are dissimilar.
It is not the cause of defiled states of other stages, because their modes of activity are contradictory.
A pure first dhyāna is the cause of a pure first dhyāna, but not the cause of defiled states, because they are dissimilar.
It is not the cause of the untainted (*anāsrava*), nor is it similar to it.
It is not the cause of the pure (*śuddha*) states of other stages, because it is the retribution (*vipāka*) of its own stage and is bound to its own stage.
All such cases should be understood in this way.
The conditions by way of cause have already been explained; the condition by way of immediate succession shall now be discussed.
Question:
How many kinds arise from each single [condition] in immediate succession?
Answer: Following the sequence of the untainted dhyānas, one gives rise to six kinds of dhyāna;
the seventh, eighth, ninth, and tenth arise, as does the dhyāna of emptiness.
From the untainted (*anāsrava*) first dhyāna, six types arise in succession: the pure (*śuddha*) and the untainted of its own level; likewise for the untainted second and third dhyānas.
From the untainted sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*), seven arise in succession:
two of its own level, four of the lower levels, and one of the higher level.
From the untainted third dhyāna, eight [minds] arise in succession:
two from its own level, two from the lower levels, and four from the higher levels.
From the untainted Infinite Consciousness Sphere, nine [minds] arise in succession:
From its own level, two; from lower levels, four; from higher levels, three.
The remaining untainted [minds] arise in succession as ten:
from its own level, two; from lower levels, four; from higher levels, four.
The pure [attainments] of the six [lower realms] arise from seven, eight, nine, ten, or eleven;
The dhyānas associated with relishing arise from two, up to ten.

Regarding "the pure [attainments] of the six arise from seven, eight, nine, ten, or eleven": the pure attainment of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception arises in succession from six [attainments].
From its own level, it is associated with *āsvādana* (tasting) and is pure (*śuddha*); from lower levels, it is fourfold.

It is pure and untainted (*anāsrava*) in the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*) and the sphere of infinite consciousness (*vijñānānantyāyatana*), but not associated with *āsvādana*, because of the absence of desire for them.
All of this should be understood as follows: all [dhyānas] are associated with the savor (*āsvādana*) of their own stage.
Regarding the statement that "the dhyānas associated with savor give rise to two, and by means of ten":

the dhyāna associated with savor gives rise in succession to two—namely, the dhyāna associated with savor and the pure (*śuddha*) dhyāna of its own stage—and no others, because they are mutually incompatible.
Thus, all [attainments] of one's own level are of two types, while those of a lower level are of one type—namely, the pure (śuddhaka). A certain person says:
"There should not be a single pure attainment of a lower level;
rather, all [attainments] associated with relishing (āsvādana) arise at the time of death."
The sequence has already been explained; the conditions (pratyaya) shall now be discussed.
Question:
How many kinds of conditions are there for each [of the dharmas]?
Answer: Pure [dhyāna], being untainted, necessarily takes all stages as its object;
defiled dhyāna associated with [afflictions] takes only its own stage as its object.

Regarding the statement that "the pure [meditations] and the untainted meditations necessarily take all stages as their objects": both the pure and the untainted meditations take all types of things in all stages as their objects.

Regarding the statement that "the defiled meditations associated with attachment take only their own stage as their objects": the meditations associated with attachment take as their objects the meditations associated with attachment and the pure meditations of their own stage; they do not take the untainted as objects because there is no craving for the untainted, nor do they delight in other stages.
The formless [attainments] lack power; they take the impure stages below as their object.
The wholesome [formless attainments] have the fundamental stages; the defiled ones are like the dhyānas of relishing. Regarding "the formless lack power;
they take the impure stages below as their object": the formless absorptions cannot take the impure phenomena of the lower stages as their objects, because they are extremely tranquil.
Question:
What is meant by the statement that the formless [attainments] cannot take the contaminated phenomena of lower stages as their objects? Answer:

The wholesome [attainments] have the fundamental dhyānas as their basis for purification, as well as the fundamental formless attainments (ārūpya) which are untainted (anāsrava). These take their own level and higher levels as objects, but not lower levels.
As for the defiled [attainments], they are like the "dhyāna of relishing" (āsvādana); as explained regarding those associated with relishing, the same applies to the formless attainments.

It is said that other qualities in the form realm, such as the immeasurables (*apramāṇa*) and so forth, necessarily have the desire realm as their object; this is what the World-Honored One has taught.

That is to say, all other qualities in the form realm—such as the spheres of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*), the spheres of totality (*kṛtsnāyatana*), and the liberations (*vimokṣa*)—have only the desire realm as their object, taking as their objects immeasurable sentient beings who suffer.
Blue and other such colors belong to this desire realm.
Why is this? Because the supernormal powers have both realms as their objects.
Question:
What is this "perfumed dhyāna" (kṣipta-dhyāna) spoken of by the Blessed One? Answer:
All four dhyānas are cultivated; the untainted (anāsrava) cultivates the tainted (sāsrava), and by the power of this untainted state, one receives the retribution of the Śuddhāvāsa heavens.
Question:
If all four dhyānas are cultivated, for what reason is there no fruit of the Śuddhāvāsa heavens within the lower three dhyānas?
Answer: If one can perfume the various dhyānas, this relies upon the fourth dhyāna;
because craving for the three stages has been exhausted, one dwells among the fruits of the Pure Abodes.
If one attains the fourth dhyāna, this is the "perfuming dhyāna" (*kṣipta-dhyāna*).
In the fourth dhyāna, the perfuming occurs first, and the others follow later.
This means that upon attaining the fourth dhyāna, one becomes free from the desires of the third dhyāna; for this reason, [the characteristics of] the lower stages do not exist there.
Among the fruits of the Śuddhāvāsa [heaven], there was one who questioned the World-Honored One regarding the existence of "knowledge resulting from aspiration" (praṇidhijñāna).
What is this? He replied:
The nature of non-attachment is immovable; this is the attainment of all meditative concentrations (*samādhi*).
By virtue of that power of concentration, one is able to give rise to the four dhyānas of the Summit (*mūrdhan*).
Among these, there are the merit-born qualities of the mind, such as the vows, knowledge, non-contention, and the foremost of eloquence.

Regarding the knowledge of vows: as one enters meditative absorption according to one's vow—whether it concerns the past, future, or present; or whether it concerns the conditioned or the unconditioned—one knows all of these completely.

One who does not engage in dispute desires that no dispute arise in the minds of others, and thus does not initiate debate; such a person has reached certainty regarding the meaning and flavor of all phenomena, being free from doubt, unimpeded, and fearless.
Question:
To which stages (bhūmi) do this knowledge resulting from aspiration (praṇidhijñāna), non-contention (araṇā), and analytical knowledge (pratisaṃvid) belong? Answer:
The third stage possesses the knowledge of aspiration; The absence of conflict relies on five stages;
Dharma, etymology, and eloquence rely on two; Two types of eloquence rely on nine.
Regarding "the third stage possesses the knowledge of aspiration": the knowledge of aspiration (*praṇidhijñāna*) is subsumed within the three stages.
The fourth dhyāna, the first dhyāna, and the desire realm.
Entering the fourth dhyāna, one knows the first dhyāna and the desire realm.

Regarding the statement that the basis for the absence of conflict (*araṇā*) consists of five stages: the absence of conflict is obtainable in five stages—the four fundamental dhyānas and the desire realm—because one desires that all beings be without conflict.

Regarding the two bases for the analytical knowledge of phenomena (*dharma-pratisaṃvid*) and the analytical knowledge of expression (*nirukti-pratisaṃvid*): the analytical knowledge of phenomena is defined as having "taste" (*rasa*) as its object; it exists in the desire realm and the Brahma world, but not in the higher stages, because those stages are free from applied and sustained thought (*vitarka-vicāra*).
The eloquence of expression (*nirukti-pratibhāna*) is the wisdom that composes words and meanings; it is also obtainable in two stages:
the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) and the world of Brahmā (*brahmaloka*).

Regarding the two types of eloquence based on the nine [stages], the eloquence of meaning (*artha-pratibhāna*) and the eloquence of application (*pratibhāna*), they are obtainable within the nine stages.
The four dhyānas, the four formless attainments, and the desire realm.

Having already explained the first dhyāna, one should know that the "access concentration" (anāgamya) and the "intermediate dhyāna" (dhyānāntara) have also been explained, as these are the attendants of the first dhyāna.
Question:
How is this concentration attained? Answer:
Through the abandonment of desire one also gives rise to it, and thereby attains pure dhyāna;
through defilement there is falling away and arising; the untainted [dhyāna] involves only the abandonment of desire.
Regarding "through the abandonment of desire one also gives rise to it, and thereby attains pure dhyāna": pure first dhyāna is attained at two times.
One should know all such cases: at the time of detachment from desire, and upon death in a higher realm and rebirth in the Brahma-world.

Regarding the defiled [attainment] obtained through falling away and through rebirth—the defiled is associated with relishing (āsvādana) and is obtained at the time of falling away; it is obtained at that moment when one falls away due to the fetters (paryavasthāna) of the desire realm or the Brahma-world.

Regarding the attainment of the first dhyāna associated with relish (*āsvādana*) at the time of its arising: it is attained when one dies from a higher plane and is reborn in the desire realm or the world of Brahmā.
All such cases regarding the first dhyāna associated with relish should be understood in this same way.
Regarding "the untainted [attainment] is acquired only when abandoning desire": the untainted [attainment] is acquired only at the time of abandoning desire.
That is to say, when a noble one attains freedom from desire, they acquire the untainted first dhyāna at that very moment.
All such matters should be understood in this way.
Question:
Who is able to eliminate afflictions through these merits?
Answer: The untainted [state] eliminates the afflictions; it is likewise found in the intermediate meditative concentrations.
All intermediate meditative concentrations are associated with the faculty of equanimity.
Regarding "the untainted [attainments] remove afflictions": the untainted first dhyāna removes the afflictions of eight stages;
all such cases should be understood in this way.

Furthermore, regarding "also the intermediate concentration" (*dhyānāntara*): the term "intermediate concentration" refers to the removal of desire for a lower stage by means of the path of preparation (*prayoga-mārga*); because it is a preparatory path, it ultimately does not give rise to the fundamental [concentration].
As long as one has not yet attained freedom from desire, nothing else can remove it.

Regarding those who associate with the faculty of equanimity (*upekṣendriya*) during all intermediate stages of meditative concentration (*dhyānāntara*), they are associated with the faculty of equanimity throughout all intermediate concentrations; ultimately, they do not attain joy, and thus fail to attain the goal.
Question:
How many types of transformation-minds (nirmāṇacitta) are there—namely, those that possess the supernormal power of the bases of psychic power (ṛddhipāda)? Answer:
8. The fruit of the four dhyānas belongs to the desire realm; the fruit of the four dhyānas belongs to the stage of the first dhyāna.
Question:
Who accomplishes these?
Answer: The transformation-mind of a lower stage accomplishes the fruit of its own seeds;
if one combines these with the three types of mind, it should be explained as belonging to the higher stages.

Regarding the accomplishment of the seeds and fruits of the transformation-mind (*nirmāṇa-citta*) of the lower stages: this means that if one accomplishes dhyāna, one accomplishes the transformation-mind of the lower stages which constitutes its fruit.
Question:
As it is said that there are four types of mind in the first dhyāna, how can one abide in a higher stage while desiring to hear or see?
How does he see and hear?
Answer: Consciousness belonging to the level of the Brahma-world manifests before him.
Question:
For how long is that accomplished? Answer:
If one were to combine these three types [of consciousness], it should be stated that they belong to the higher stages (*ūrdhvabhūmi*).
When those consciousnesses—whether visual, olfactory, auditory, or tactile—are present before one, at that time one possesses them;
when they are not present and have ceased, at that time one does not possess them.
*Abhidharmahṛdaya-śāstra*, Fascicle Three;

Composed by the Venerable Dharmasri.

In the first year of the Taiyuan era of the Jin dynasty, Saṃghadeva, together with Huiyuan, translated [this work] at Mount Lu. Chapter Eight: The Sūtra Section. The Section on Concentration has already been explained; the Section on the Sūtras shall now be discussed.
The subtle meaning of the sūtras as taught by the Omniscient One—this I shall now expound; you should listen with a virtuous mind.
Although all the meanings of the Abhidharma and the sūtras exist, the various sūtras ought to be analyzed in detail; I shall now do so.
The World-Honored One has spoken of the three realms:
the realm of desire, the realm of form, and the formless realm.
Question:
What is this? The answer is:
There are ten abodes in the desire realm, and seventeen are taught in the form realm.
In the formless realm there are four; the three realms of existence are likewise.
Regarding "the ten abodes in the desire realm": these are the ten abodes in the desire realm:
hell-beings, animals, hungry ghosts, humans, and the six heavens of the desire realm—the Four Great Kings, the Thirty-three Gods, Yāma, Tuṣita, Nirmāṇarati, and Paranirmita-vaśavartin.

These sentient beings give rise to thoughts of desire; because all objects obtainable within this realm are entirely associated with sensual passion, it is therefore called the "Desire Realm" (kāmadhātu).
Question:
What is the "Form Realm" (rūpadhātu)?
Answer: Seventeen [levels] are taught for the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*).

Regarding the statement that seventeen are taught for the realm of form: they are the Brahmakāyika, Brahmapurohita, Parīttābha, Apramāṇābha, Ābhāsvara, Parīttaśubha, Apramāṇaśubha, Śubhakṛtsna, Anabhraka, Puṇyaprasava, Bṛhatphala, Asaṃjñisattva, Avṛha, Atapa, Sudṛśa, Sudarśana, and Akaniṣṭha.

In this realm, no perception of desire arises; rather, there is only the attainment of an exceedingly sublime form that is neither male nor female in shape. Therefore, it is called the Form Realm (*rūpadhātu*).
Regarding the four within the Formless Realm, there are four levels in the Formless Realm:
abiding in the Sphere of Infinite Space, the Sphere of Infinite Consciousness, the Sphere of Nothingness, and the Sphere of Neither Perception nor Non-perception.
Since there is no form (*rūpa*) in this place, and because one is free from desire for form, it is therefore called the Formless Realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).
Question:

The Blessed One has spoken of the three existences (*bhava*): the existence of desire (*kāmadhātu-bhava*), the existence of form (*rūpadhātu-bhava*), and the existence of the formless (*ārūpyadhātu-bhava*).
What does this mean? Answer:
The three realms of existence (*tribhava*) are likewise so; that is, the aforementioned distinctions of the three realms are themselves the three realms of existence.
Question:
As the Blessed One has taught the seven stations of consciousness, what are they? Answer:

The "fortunate realms" (sugati) consist of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), the first three stages of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), and likewise the first three stages of the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*);
through wisdom, one knows these as the stations of consciousness (*vijñānasthiti*).

Within this desire realm, those counted as fortunate destinies include human beings and the six classes of gods of the desire realm; [the same applies to] the first three stages of the form realm and the first three stages of the formless realm.

From the first dhyāna stage there are three [types of beings] in the second dhyāna stage; from the second dhyāna stage there are three in the third dhyāna stage; and from the third dhyāna stage there are nine in the fourth dhyāna stage.
Among these, the first three stages and the first three formless stages are designated as the seven stations of consciousness (*vijñānasthiti*).

Why is this? Because consciousness is not destroyed [therein], yet it is destroyed by the suffering and pain within the miserable realms (apāya), it cannot be established as a station of consciousness (vijñānasthiti).
Furthermore, because it is destroyed by the attainment of non-conception (asaṃjñi-samāpatti) in the fourth dhyāna, it also cannot be established as a station of consciousness.

Because the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception and the attainment of cessation are subject to destruction, they cannot be established as stations of consciousness; therefore, they are not mentioned.
The Peak of Existence (bhavāgra) and the non-percipient beings—these nine are called the abodes of sentient beings.
The four contaminated aggregates are said to be the four stations of consciousness.

Regarding the first point, the statement that there are nine abodes of sentient beings including the non-percipient beings of the Peak of Existence: these seven stations of consciousness, along with the non-percipient beings and the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, are what are called the nine abodes of sentient beings.
Sentient beings dwell therein; therefore, they are called "abodes of sentient beings" (*sattvāvāsa*).

As for the statement that "the four contaminated aggregates (*skandha*) are the four stations of consciousness (*vijñānasthiti*)," this means that when the continuity of consciousness has these as its companions—namely, contaminated form (*rūpa*), feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), and formations (*saṃskāra*)"—therefore, they are called "stations of consciousness."
Question:
The Blessed One has taught the twelve-linked dependent origination (*dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda*).
Its characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) should also be explained.
Answer: All afflictions and karmas, possessing substantiality, arise gradually;
this is called "having branches," which refers to the various births of sentient beings.
Among these, the afflictions are ignorance (*avidyā*), craving (*tṛṣṇā*), and grasping (*upādāna*).
Those designated as "action" (*karma*) are formative forces (*saṃskāra*) and existence (*bhava*).
Those designated as "substance" (*vastu*) are the remaining members.

All sentient beings arise gradually; based upon the substance (tattva), afflictions are established; that which is produced by afflictions is karma, and that which is produced by karma is the substance. Therefore, there are twelve kinds of conceptualization.
Question:
Do these factors (aṅga) function simultaneously, or do they arise gradually? Answer:
It is not simultaneous.
The twelve aggregates of suffering are explained as having twelve branches, with ignorance at the head.
These are established in sequence for one who undergoes birth and death.
Regarding the past and the future, the eight [limbs] are explained as being situated in the middle. These limbs are established in their sequential order:

therein, when [a state] is about to arise, all afflictions that are co-existent and associated are called ignorance (*avidyā*); by means of this, one performs karma, and the fruit produced by that karma is volitional formations (*saṃskāra*). That which is the seed of its arising is consciousness (*vijñāna*); the continuity of the four aggregates (*skandha*) that arise together with it is name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*).

Among these, with the eye as the primary basis, the various faculties constitute the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*). The conjunction of the faculties, their objects, and consciousness is contact (*sparśa*). The sensation produced by contact is feeling (*vedanā*). Attachment to feeling is craving (*tṛṣṇā*). The exertion involved in the equipment for feeling is grasping (*upādāna*). The karma created through that exertion is becoming (*bhava*). The further undergoing of results therein is birth (*jāti*). Within that birth, the arising of immeasurable calamities is aging and death (*jarāmaraṇa*).
Thus, among all births within these branches of existence (*bhavāṅga*), two are subsumed under the past, two under the future, and eight are subsumed within the present birth.
Question:
The Blessed One spoke of the six elements (*ṣaḍdhātu*); how are these [to be understood]?
Answer: The great elements are said to be four, together with the tainted consciousness;
they are known as being within form. These realms are taught to be the basis for arising.
Regarding the statement, "The great elements are four, as well as contaminated consciousness; that which is known between form [and consciousness] is the intermediate":
the four great elements are earth, water, fire, and wind.
Contaminated consciousness and form can be known in the interval; these six factors are called "elements" (*dhātu*).
Question:
For what reason are six elements taught among the many dharmas? Answer:
This realm is said to be the root of birth.

These six factors are the root of saṃsāra; herein there is the notion of a person (*pudgala*). Within this, the body arises from earth, is moistened by water, matured by fire, cleared of putrefaction by wind, and sustained by food and drink within the space; it functions through the movement of wind and is established by consciousness (*vijñāna*) entering and exiting.
In this context, the arising of the notion of a "person" (pudgala) is the nature of saṃsāra; therefore, it is called a "realm" (dhātu).
Question:
The Blessed One has taught the Four Noble Truths; what are their characteristics?
Answer: If conditioned phenomena possess a fruit, they are tainted and are called suffering;
if they possess a cause, they are accumulation. The cessation of suffering is called extinction.

Regarding the statement that "all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) which possess results and are outflowing (*sāsrava*) are called suffering": all outflowing phenomena arise from the cause of volitional formations (*saṃskāra*) and also produce all manner of suffering and affliction; therefore, all conditioned phenomena are said to be the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkha-satya*).

If there is that which has a cause, it is conditioned by practice; all contaminated formations (*sāsrava-saṃskāra*) have others as their causes, and for this reason, all formations are called the Truth of Practice (*samudaya-satya*).
It is like one woman who is called both "mother" and "daughter," depending on her relation to what precedes and follows her.

In this way, these contaminated formations (*sāsrava-saṃskāra*) are also called the truth of suffering (*duḥkha-satya*) and the truth of origination (*samudaya-satya*), because they have arisen or will arise.
That which is the exhaustion of suffering is called cessation (*nirodha*); the extinction, subsiding, and stopping of all contaminated formations is called the truth of cessation (*nirodha-satya*).
If there is untainted conduct, it is called the Truth of the Path;
because it serves two purposes, one who sees attachment will know the subtle.
If untainted conduct is called the Truth of the Path, then all untainted conduct is said to be the Truth of the Path.
Why is this? Because at the time of the cessation of suffering, all these factors are fully present.
Question:
For what reason are the truths (satya) taught? Answer:
It is for two purposes.
The truths are explained by way of two aspects:
the reality of specific characteristics that is non-erroneous, and the intention that one’s seeing of them is non-erroneous.
Question:
Just as the cause precedes the effect, for what reason does the World-Honored One first speak of the effect and later speak of the cause?
Answer: When one perceives the attachment, one thereby knows the subtle.

Although the Noble Truths involve the prior cultivation of the truth of origination and the subsequent realization of the truth of suffering, and the prior cultivation of the path and the subsequent attainment of cessation, one should nonetheless first perceive the truth of suffering and subsequently perceive the truth of origination; likewise, one should first perceive the truth of cessation and subsequently perceive the truth of the path.
Why is this? Suffering is coarse while its origin is subtle; cessation is coarse while the path is subtle.
Therefore, the World-Honored One first taught the Truth of Suffering and later the Truth of Origin; he first taught the Truth of Cessation and later the Truth of the Path.
Question:
The Blessed One has spoken of the four noble fruits of the śramaṇa; how many kinds are there? Answer:
There are six kinds of noble fruits (*āryaphala*); the most excellent resides in the nine stages, while the third resides in the six stages; both rely upon the *anāgāmya*.

Regarding "there are six kinds of noble fruits": these are the six types of the four fruits of śrāmaṇya, consisting of the five untainted aggregates (*anāsravaskandha*) and cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṃkhyānirodha*).
Question:
By which stages (bhūmi) are the four fruits of śrāmaṇya subsumed? Answer:
The supreme [attainment] resides in the nine stages.
This supreme state is the fruit of non-attachment and is comprised within these nine stages:
the four fundamental dhyānas, the three formless attainments, the preliminary stage (anāgamya), and the intermediate stage (dhyānāntara).
Regarding the third point, "abiding in the sixth stage": the fruit of non-returner (anāgāmiphala) is subsumed within the six stages;

it comprises the four dhyānas, the preliminary stage (anāgamya), and the intermediate dhyāna (dhyānāntara), but not the formless realms (ārūpya), because there is no knowledge of phenomena (dharmajñāna) therein.
Regarding those that both rely on the future: the fruit of *srotāpanna* and the fruit of *sakṛdāgāmin* are subsumed under future dhyāna because they have not yet abandoned desire.
Question:

The World-Honored One taught four paths: the difficult path with slow super-knowledge (*duḥkhā pratipad dhandhābhijñā*), the difficult path with quick super-knowledge (*duḥkhā pratipad kṣiprābhijñā*), the pleasant path with slow super-knowledge (*sukhā pratipad dhandhābhijñā*), and the pleasant path with quick super-knowledge (*sukhā pratipad kṣiprābhijñā*).
What are its characteristics? Answer:
Arising from the practice of faith in all dharmas, it is free from afflictions and characterized by slowness of thought.
Regarding "practicing all dharmas through the practice of dharma, there is the thought of being free from afflictions quickly":

regarding "practicing all dharmas through the practice of faith, there is the thought of being free from afflictions slowly," practicing the untainted (anāsrava) dharmas through the practice of faith is not quick; it is slow because it is comprised of those with dull faculties.

If one receives this, it should be known that those liberated by faith (*śraddhādhimukta*) and those liberated by time (*samayavimukta*) also receive it, because they share the same dull faculties (*mṛdvindriya*).

Regarding "from the dharma-practitioner (*dharmānusārin*), there is the thought of the swift absence of afflictions in all dharmas": from the untainted (*anāsrava*) dharmas of the dharma-practitioner, that which is comprised by those of sharp faculties (*tīkṣṇendriya*) is "swift."
If one accepts this, it should be known that those with views and those liberated at non-specific times also accept it, because they possess identical sharp faculties.
Within the stages of the fundamental dhyānas, one perceives the notion of pleasure as being merely conventional, because it is slight and difficult to obtain; all else is the notion of suffering.

Regarding "knowing the perception of the pleasure of conventional designations within the stages of the fundamental dhyānas": this refers to the teaching that the path is pleasant for those of both sharp and dull faculties within the four fundamental dhyānas. Why is this so?
Because śamatha and vipaśyanā guide [the path] equally and because it is pleasant to practice;

as for "the small and the difficult-to-attain," all others are the perception of suffering (duḥkha-saṃjñā), meaning that the untainted (anāsrava) states subsumed under the other stages are the perception of suffering.
Why is this? Because they are minor.

In the preparatory dhyāna (*anāgāmya-dhyāna*) and the intermediate dhyāna (*dhyānāntara*), the path of cessation is minor; in the formless attainments (*ārūpya*), observation is minor. Therefore, because suffering is extreme, exclusively difficult to transcend, and minor, it is called "suffering."
Question:

The Blessed One has spoken of the four kinds of unshakable confidence (*aveccappasāda*): unshakable confidence in the Buddha, and unshakable confidence in the Dharma, the Saṅgha, and the noble precepts (*ariya-sīla*).
What does this mean?
Answer: Self-awakening, the Dharma of the śrāvakas, liberation, as well as other causes,
pure and stainless faith, noble ethical discipline, and certainty.

Regarding "the self-awakened Śrāvaka’s liberation from the Dharma, as well as the pure and stainless faith resulting from other causes": the "self-awakened" refers to a Buddha; that Buddha is subsumed within the fruit of non-attachment.

The qualities of those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) are the Buddha-dharma; if one possesses untainted faith (*anāsrava-śraddhā*) in these dharmas, this is called "unshakable purity toward the Buddha" (*buddhe 'vetyaprasāda*).
As for the śrāvakas who have already attained realization, their qualities of both training (*śaikṣa*) and beyond training are called the śrāvaka-dharma.
If there is untainted faith (*anāsrava-śraddhā*) toward this Dharma, it is called the indestructible confidence in the Saṃgha.

Untainted faith in *nirvāṇa*, as well as faith in other conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*)—such as faith in the truths of suffering and its origin, faith in the untainted merits of a Bodhisattva, and faith in the dharmas of those in training (*śaikṣa*), those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), and Pratyekabuddhas—is called the indestructible confidence in the Dharma.
The noble precepts are the untainted precepts; these are called the unshakable confidence in the precepts.
Question:
For what reason is unshakable confidence exclusively untainted and not tainted?
Answer: And it is definitive.
This is definitive because it arises from right view.
Untainted faith and untainted precepts are definitively untainted.
Tainted faith is destroyed by lack of faith, and tainted precepts are destroyed by non-precepts; therefore, they are not definitive.
The untainted (*anāsrava*) and indestructible [faith] persists into future lives; because it is thus determined, the indestructible purities (*akopya-prasāda*) are exclusively untainted.
Question:

The Blessed One has taught that there are four types of cultivation of concentration (*samādhi-bhāvanā*): there is the cultivation of concentration for dwelling in happiness in the present life (*dṛṣṭadharmasukhavihāra*), the cultivation of concentration for knowledge and vision (*jñānadarśana*), the cultivation of concentration for the discernment of wisdom (*prajñā-vibhāga*), and the cultivation of concentration for the exhaustion of the outflows (*āsravakṣaya*).
What are its characteristics? Answer:
If there is goodness in the first dhyāna, it is said that this present life is happiness.
If one knows [the nature] of birth and death, this is called "knowledge and vision.
If it is rightly said that the first dhyāna is happiness in the present life, then the pure and untainted first dhyāna can attain dwelling in happiness in the present life.

If one knows [the nature] within birth and death, this is called "knowledge and vision. The supernormal power of knowledge regarding birth and death is said to be the meditative concentration cultivated in reliance upon the five aggregates.
One should know that the discernment of wisdom seeks to attain all merits;
the diamond-like fourth dhyāna is what is termed the "exhaustion of outflows" (āsravakṣaya).
One should understand through wise discernment that those who seek to attain all merits produce merit through skillful means; this is called the morality of the desire realm.
The merits of hearing, reflection, and cultivation comprise all wholesome dharmas of the form and formless realms.
All untainted conditioned phenomena are the cultivation of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and the analytical wisdom (*prajñā*).

That which is called the "diamond-like fourth dhyāna" of one whose outflows are exhausted (*āsravakṣaya*) is associated with and co-existent with the final mind of a trainee (*śaikṣa*); it is subsumed under the fourth dhyāna, and this is described as the exhaustion of outflows through the cultivation of meditative concentration.
What is the meaning?
This has been explained by the Tathāgata himself.
Question:
The World-Honored One has taught the four bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*), the four right efforts (*samyakprahāṇa*), and the four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*).
Their characteristics should also be explained. Answer:

Wholesome conditioned phenomena, arising through the pursuit of skillful means, the Buddha has called the bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*), and he has also manifested them as the right abandonments (*samyakprahāṇa*).

Regarding "wholesome conditioned phenomena, arising through the pursuit of skillful means, the Buddha has called the bases of psychic power": the arising through the pursuit of skillful means is as previously explained in the analysis of the cultivation of concentration and wisdom; all these are the bases of psychic power because they are the vehicle for the attainment of *ṛddhi*.
That which is also manifested as right effort (*samyakprahāṇa*) is precisely all these virtues spoken of as the right abandonments.
They are also the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*), and the four noble lineages (*āryavaṃśa*) are likewise so;
they arise through the power of grace, as taught by those Noble Ones.
"That which is also the application of mindfulness" means that this very dharma is also called an application of mindfulness.
Question:
The World-Honored One spoke of the four noble lineages; what are these?
Answer: The four noble lineages (āryavaṃśa) are likewise; that is, these very dharmas are also called the four noble lineages.
Question:

Why is this? It is because all these virtues are described as the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*), the right efforts (*samyakprahāṇa*), the bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*), and the noble lineages (*āryavaṃśa*).
Answer: They are so called because they possess the power of grace that gives rise to what is taught by the Noble Ones.
These dharmas arise through the power of concentration and abide by means of concentration; therefore, they are called the bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*).
Because they arise through the power of diligence, they are called the right efforts (*samyakprahāṇa*).
Because they arise through the power of mindfulness, they are called the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*).
Because they arise through the power of fewness of desires and contentment, they are called the noble lineages (*āryavaṃśa*).
Having already analyzed the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*) collectively, their individual characteristics shall now be explained.
Pure faith, diligence, mindfulness, Joy, wisdom, and equanimity;
Vigilance, reflection, ethical discipline, concentration— These dharmas are called the factors of the path (mārgāṅga).
These ten dharmas constitute the factors of the path, and nothing else.

Among these, faith is the faculty of faith and the power of faith; diligence is the four right efforts, the faculty of diligence, the power of diligence, the awakening factor of diligence, and right exertion.
Mindfulness is the faculty of mindfulness, the power of mindfulness, the factor of enlightenment of mindfulness, and right mindfulness.
Joy is the factor of enlightenment of joy.
Wisdom consists of the four foundations of mindfulness, the faculty of wisdom, the power of wisdom, the factor of enlightenment of investigation of phenomena, and right view.
Reliance is the factor of enlightenment of investigation;
protection is the factor of enlightenment of energy;
and reflection is right intention.
Morality consists of right speech, right action, and right livelihood.
Concentration consists of the four bases of power, the faculty of concentration, the power of concentration, the factor of enlightenment that is concentration, and right concentration.
Question:
Why are these dharmas analyzed in such various ways? Answer:

Regarding the bases, the skillful means, and the single mind; for those of dull faculties and sharp faculties, on the path of seeing and the path of cultivation—the Buddha taught the thirty-seven [factors].
As for "bases" (*sthāna*): because right mindfulness is established upon objects, they are called applications of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*).
Regarding "skillful means" (upāya), because they are right skillful means, they are called the right efforts (samyakprahāṇa).
Regarding "one-pointedness of mind," because one establishes a single intent, they are called the bases of power (ṛddhipāda).
Because the faculties of a dull or weak mind are attained, they are called the faculties (indriya).
For those of sharp faculties, they are called "powers" because they are attained through the faculty of sharpness.
For those on the path of seeing, they are called "path factors" because they are attained on the path of seeing.
For those on the path of cultivation, they are called "factors of enlightenment" because they are attained on the path of cultivation.
This is called "due to the analysis of phenomena.
The Buddha taught the thirty-seven [limbs of enlightenment]; it is because of these ten phenomena that the Buddha taught the thirty-seven.
Question:
In which stages (*bhūmi*) are these factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa*) included? Answer:
In the second dhyāna and its preparatory stage (*anāgamya*), thirty-six are said to be present.
"Three, four, three, and five; the intermediate dhyāna is likewise.

Regarding 'the second dhyāna has thirty-six in the future': because the second dhyāna lacks right intention (*samyak-saṃkalpa*), and the preparatory dhyāna (*anāgamya*) lacks the factor of joy (*prīti-saṃbodhyaṅga*), the remainder consists of three, four, three, and five."

The intermediate dhyāna is likewise: in the third and fourth dhyānas and the intermediate dhyāna, there is no factor of joy (prīti) and no right intention (samyak-saṃkalpa); the remaining factors are present.
The first [dhyāna] possesses all; the three empties have thirty-one;
the supreme has twenty-one; the desire realm has twenty-two.
